Reading noteBased on chapter 1, “Security today” (book pp. 3–14). Figures are embedded from the book PDF in this repository.
The 60-second takeaway

Working software is not necessarily safe software.

The opening chapter shifts your focus from what an application does to what it must protect. Security is a nonfunctional requirement that has to be designed across the whole system—not bolted on after the feature is finished.

01

What Spring Security does

Spring Security is the customizable application-security framework for Spring projects. It helps developers implement identity checks, access rules, and defenses against common attacks using familiar Spring patterns: beans, configuration, and annotations.

ID

Authentication

Establish who—or what—is making a request.

✓

Authorization

Decide which actions and resources that identity may access.

✳

Protection

Apply framework support against common application-level attacks.

Important distinction. Adding the framework does not automatically make an application secure. Developers must configure the right rules for their own endpoints, data, and architecture; Spring Security is a toolbox, not a guarantee.
02

What “secure” really means

An application handles information people care about: email addresses, financial details, credentials, and more. Protecting it means preventing unauthorized reading, modification, interception, or use of both data and functionality.

First question

Who are you?

Authentication identifies the person or service asking to act.

Identity before access
Second question

What may you do?

Authorization evaluates permissions for a resource or operation.

Access follows identity

Security also covers data at rest (stored information), data in transit (messages between components), and even sensitive material left in application memory. Credentials must be handled deliberately; a printer or another service should not receive a user’s full privileges just to perform one limited task.

03

Security has layers

The chapter separates application-level protection from the security of the network, operating system, virtual machines, containers, and data stores. Spring Security mainly operates at the application layer. Each other layer still needs its own defenses.

ApplicationVerify identities, enforce access rules, protect endpoints and methods.
SystemProtect the runtime, persistence, and the processes your app relies on.
InfrastructureSecure networks, machines, operating systems, and deployment environments.
Practical implication. In a multi-service system, validate the caller and protect traffic even between services you own. A network location or a supposedly trusted upstream component is not proof of identity.
04

Why it matters

Weak security has a cost beyond the immediate technical incident. Exposed information, unauthorized payments, and data shown to the wrong user can damage trust, finances, and sometimes legal standing.

Data exposure

Internal information leaks out

A back-office app reveals material intended only for the organization. The impact reaches employees, customers, and the business.

Wrong action

A charge belongs to someone else

A ride-sharing user sees a payment for a trip they never took. Refunding it may not restore confidence.

Wrong user

A banking app displays another customer’s transactions

An authorization mistake exposes sensitive records and can have serious trust and regulatory consequences.

The author’s central advice: address security early and assess risk deliberately. Small mistakes—such as revealing secrets in logs or error messages—can have outsized consequences.

</>

A tiny companion example

Chapter 1 is conceptual and contains no Java code listings. This original, illustrative Spring Boot 3 / Spring Security 6 example makes its authentication-versus-authorization distinction concrete. It is not copied from the book.

NOTEAdd spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-security to a Spring Boot project. This is a teaching example, not a production-ready authentication design.
SecurityConfig.java · illustrative example
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/public").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().authenticated())
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .build();
  }
}

@RestController
class DemoController {
  @GetMapping("/public")
  String publicPage() { return "Anyone can read this"; }

  @GetMapping("/private")
  String privatePage() { return "Authenticated users only"; }
}
  1. /public is accessible without signing in.
  2. Every other request, including /private, requires an authenticated identity.
  3. HTTP Basic is enabled only to keep the demo short; use it only over HTTPS. Configure a real identity source and appropriate access rules in production. The example does not disable CSRF protection.
✓

Keep these ideas

01Security is a design concern from the start, not a finishing touch.
02Spring Security supports application-level protection; it does not replace other layers.
03Authentication asks who; authorization asks what they may do.
04Good defaults help, but developers remain responsible for the actual configuration.

Check your understanding

Does adding Spring Security make an app secure by itself?

No. The developer must configure and test protection for the application’s real resources, users, and architecture.

Why secure service-to-service requests?

Another service or host may be compromised, and network traffic may be intercepted. A request’s source still needs to be validated.

What comes after chapter 1?

Chapter 2 starts a hands-on Spring Security project. Later chapters explore authentication, authorization, OAuth 2/OpenID Connect, reactive applications, and testing.

From concept
to code.

The second chapter builds a tiny protected endpoint, traces the authentication pipeline, and shows how to replace Spring Boot’s defaults—one component at a time.

Chapter two

The big picture01 / First application02 / Authentication flow03 / Override defaults04 / Design choicesQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 2, “Hello, Spring Security” (book pp. 15–39). The figures below come from the provided PDF; the runnable code is newly written.
The 60-second takeaway

Spring Boot starts secure; you make the rules yours.

Add the web and security starters and Spring Boot protects your endpoints by default. Chapter 2 moves from that first experience to the components behind authentication, then shows how a SecurityFilterChain, user service, password encoder, and optional custom provider fit together.

01

Your first secured endpoint

Create a Spring Boot 3 project with two dependencies: spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-security. A simple GET /hello handler is enough to see the default protection in action.

pom.xml · dependencies inside a Spring Boot Maven project
<dependencies>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-web</artifactId>
  </dependency>
  <dependency>
    <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
    <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-security</artifactId>
  </dependency>
</dependencies>
DemoApplication.java · default-security demo
import org.springframework.boot.SpringApplication;
import org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.SpringBootApplication;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@SpringBootApplication
public class DemoApplication {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    SpringApplication.run(DemoApplication.class, args);
  }
}

@RestController
class HelloController {
  @GetMapping("/hello")
  String hello() { return "Hello!"; }
}
01 / StartSpring Boot logs a generated password for the default user named user.
02 / No credentialsA cURL request to /hello receives 401 Unauthorized.
03 / AuthenticateSend the username and generated password with HTTP Basic; the response is 200 OK and Hello!.
Terminal · local demonstration
# First request: expect 401 Unauthorized
curl -i http://localhost:8080/hello

# Replace with the password printed in your application log
curl -i -u "user:YOUR_GENERATED_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello
SAFETYHTTP Basic sends Base64-encoded credentials, not encrypted credentials. Use HTTPS whenever traffic leaves your local machine. The generated user is for development, not a production identity system. A browser may show a login form instead of an HTTP Basic prompt because the defaults include form login too.
02

Follow the authentication flow

Chapter 2 names the collaborators behind that successful request. The filter receives it; the manager delegates; a provider performs the check using user details and password verification. On success, the result is held in a security context for the request.

Authentication filterIntercepts the request and starts authentication.
AuthenticationManagerCoordinates the process and delegates to a provider.
AuthenticationProviderChecks the credentials according to its authentication logic.
UserDetailsServiceLoads information about a user; the book’s first custom example uses an in-memory implementation.
PasswordEncoderEncodes and verifies passwords; it must agree with the way stored passwords were encoded.
SecurityContextHolds authentication information after a successful check, typically for the current request.
Remember the distinction. Authentication determines identity. Endpoint authorization then decides whether that authenticated identity is allowed to call a resource.
03

Replace the defaults deliberately

The chapter shows how to declare your own UserDetailsService, PasswordEncoder, and SecurityFilterChain beans. The first two control users and password checks; the filter chain controls authentication methods and endpoint access rules.

Identity configuration

Who can sign in?

Supply user details and a compatible password encoder. The in-memory manager is useful for learning, but not a production user store.

Web configuration

Which requests pass?

Use HttpSecurity to build a SecurityFilterChain; authenticated() requires a login, while permitAll() makes a route public.

The book uses NoOpPasswordEncoder with cleartext example passwords to isolate the concept. Do not adopt that choice in a real system. The companion example below uses BCrypt and reads a local demo password from an environment variable instead.

SecurityConfig.java · safer learning adaptation
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class SecurityConfig {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
  }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService userDetailsService(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    String secret = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (secret == null || secret.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for the local demo");
    }
    var user = User.withUsername("learner")
        .password(encoder.encode(secret))
        .authorities("read")
        .build();
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(user);
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .build();
  }
}

Add this file to the same package as DemoApplication, set DEMO_PASSWORD before starting the app, and call /hello with curl -u "learner:$DEMO_PASSWORD" for a local-only exercise. Do not leave demo users or environment-provided example passwords in a deployed service. This example retains Spring Security’s CSRF protection and uses only a GET endpoint.

04

Choose a maintainable design

The chapter explores more than one configuration style. You can publish components as Spring beans, or register some of them directly through HttpSecurity. Avoid mixing styles without a reason; split large configurations by responsibility.

A

Use beans when useful

A bean can be injected elsewhere and keeps dependencies explicit.

B

Customize only when needed

Implement AuthenticationProvider if the built-in authentication approach does not fit; keep user lookup and password checks separate when possible.

C

Split responsibilities

Separate user management from web authorization as configurations grow.

One rule of thumb. Use a consistent Spring Security 6 configuration style. This chapter uses SecurityFilterChain beans, not the older WebSecurityConfigurerAdapter pattern.
✓

Keep these ideas

01The security starter protects endpoints by default, with a generated development user.
02A filter, manager, provider, user service, encoder, and security context cooperate during authentication.
03SecurityFilterChain defines the web rules; authenticated() and permitAll() express different access policies.
04Learning shortcuts such as cleartext passwords and NoOp encoding must not become production defaults.

Check your understanding

Why does the default /hello return 401 in cURL?

The security dependency enables protection for endpoints by default. Without valid credentials, the request cannot be authenticated.

What happens if you replace the default user service?

Supply users and ensure stored passwords can be checked with a compatible password encoder. The book demonstrates both pieces together.

When would you write an AuthenticationProvider?

When the built-in authentication logic does not fit your requirements. It receives authentication requests and decides whether they succeed; keep responsibilities separated when possible.

Chapter 03 · Managing users

Know your
users.

Now that the authentication flow makes sense, zoom in on its user-management side: how Spring Security describes a user, finds them, and manages their account.

4 connected contracts4 original figuresEmbedded Java & SQL
The user-management family
UserDetailsManagerWRITE
UserDetailsServiceLOOKUP
UserDetails + authoritiesIDENTITY

Different contracts. Different responsibilities.

Chapter three

The big picture01 / Four contracts02 / Describe a user03 / Load a user04 / Choose storageQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 3, “Managing users” (book pp. 43–67). Figures are from the supplied PDF; code here is an original teaching adaptation.
The 60-second takeaway

Authentication needs a way to find and describe a user.

Spring Security works through small Java contracts. UserDetails represents the account, GrantedAuthority names its privileges, UserDetailsService finds it by username, and UserDetailsManager adds account-management operations. You can implement them yourself or choose a provided implementation.

01

Four contracts, one flow

Chapter 2 introduced the full authentication pipeline. Chapter 3 focuses on the piece that supplies user information to the authentication provider. The password encoder still checks credentials; its details are the subject of chapter 4.

UserDetailsThe account data Spring Security understands: username, password, authorities, and account status.
GrantedAuthorityA named privilege, such as READ, carried by a user.
UserDetailsServiceA read-only lookup contract: load a user by username or report that no such user exists.
UserDetailsManagerExtends that lookup contract with methods to create, update, delete, or change a user’s password.
02

Describe the account

UserDetails exposes a username, an encoded password, a collection of authorities, and four status flags: non-expired account, non-locked account, non-expired credentials, and enabled account. A false status can prevent successful authentication.

Privileges

What may this user do?

GrantedAuthority#getAuthority() provides a name you can refer to in access rules, for example READ or WRITE.

One user → one or more authorities
Account state

May this account sign in?

The four status methods let an account be locked, disabled, or expired. Return true for statuses your application does not restrict.

False → account is not usable

For simple accounts, Spring Security’s User builder already implements UserDetails. For more complex domain models, an adapter class can wrap a persistence entity instead of mixing JPA and security responsibilities in one class.

Important nuance. Authorities describe a user’s privileges; defining one does not automatically protect an endpoint. Your authorization rules must actually check it. Never store a cleartext password merely because a short example does.
03

Find the user by username

The one method on UserDetailsService is loadUserByUsername(String username). It returns a UserDetails instance, or throws UsernameNotFoundException if the account does not exist. The provider calls it as part of authentication.

This original example replaces the Chapter 2 SecurityConfig.java file (do not register both configurations). Keep the same DemoApplication.java and web/security starter dependencies. It uses the standard User builder to avoid reimplementing every UserDetails method, and a small custom service to demonstrate the lookup contract.

UserManagementConfig.java · custom lookup demo
import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetails;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UsernameNotFoundException;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class UserManagementConfig {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
  }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService userDetailsService(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    String secret = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (secret == null || secret.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for the local demo");
    }
    UserDetails learner = User.withUsername("learner")
        .password(encoder.encode(secret))
        .authorities("READ")
        .build();
    return new MapUserDetailsService(Map.of(learner.getUsername(), learner));
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .build();
  }
}

class MapUserDetailsService implements UserDetailsService {
  private final Map<String, UserDetails> users;

  MapUserDetailsService(Map<String, UserDetails> users) {
    this.users = Map.copyOf(users);
  }

  @Override
  public UserDetails loadUserByUsername(String username) {
    UserDetails user = users.get(username);
    if (user == null) throw new UsernameNotFoundException("User not found");
    return user;
  }
}
  1. The user is built with an encoded password and the READ authority; the service is a bean.
  2. The custom lookup returns that user or throws UsernameNotFoundException.
  3. Set DEMO_PASSWORD before starting the application and try curl -u "learner:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello locally. Use HTTPS for any non-local traffic. This is not a production user store.
04

Pick the right user store

If your app must also create, update, or remove accounts, use the broader UserDetailsManager contract. Spring Security offers implementations for in-memory users, JDBC-backed SQL users, and LDAP directories.

M

In memory

InMemoryUserDetailsManager is convenient for examples and tests; its data is not a durable account database.

DB

JDBC

JdbcUserDetailsManager reads and manages users in SQL via a DataSource; default queries expect users and authorities tables.

L

LDAP

LdapUserDetailsManager connects the contract to an LDAP directory, with context and username mapping to configure.

The JDBC option can be registered with a DataSource. The next fragments show the shape of its bean and its default table names; they are not a complete standalone project. You also need a JDBC starter and driver, a configured data source, schema initialization, actual user rows with safely encoded passwords, and a matching PasswordEncoder.

JDBC bean · alternative user store
@Bean
UserDetailsService userDetailsService(DataSource dataSource) {
  return new JdbcUserDetailsManager(dataSource);
}
schema.sql · illustrative default table shape
CREATE TABLE users (
  username VARCHAR(50) PRIMARY KEY,
  password VARCHAR(255) NOT NULL,
  enabled BOOLEAN NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE authorities (
  username VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  authority VARCHAR(50) NOT NULL,
  CONSTRAINT fk_authorities_users FOREIGN KEY (username)
    REFERENCES users(username),
  CONSTRAINT uk_authorities UNIQUE (username, authority)
);
NOTEThe book’s database and LDAP examples use cleartext passwords with NoOpPasswordEncoder to keep attention on user management. That is a teaching shortcut, not an acceptable production credential strategy. Provide a robust password encoder and protect directory/database connections.
✓

Keep these ideas

01UserDetails describes an account; GrantedAuthority names a privilege.
02UserDetailsService loads a user by username; it does not need to manage accounts.
03UserDetailsManager adds account changes and comes in memory, JDBC, and LDAP flavors.
04Keep persistence models and security adapters separate when that makes the design clearer.

Check your understanding

What does loadUserByUsername() do when no user exists?

It throws UsernameNotFoundException. Authentication can then fail without returning a made-up account.

Does granting READ automatically protect an endpoint?

No. It places a privilege on the user; an authorization rule must check that privilege before it affects access.

When should you use UserDetailsManager instead of only UserDetailsService?

When your application also needs operations such as creating, updating, deleting, or changing a user’s password.

Chapter 04 · Managing passwords

Keep secrets
secret.

Chapter four turns from finding users to verifying their passwords. Learn the encoder contract, choose an appropriate password hash, and distinguish hashing from reversible encryption.

PasswordEncoder explained4 original figures2 Java demos
The password check
Entered passwordRAW
PasswordEncoder.matches()VERIFY
Stored password hashONE-WAY

Verify the input; do not recover the password.

Chapter four

The big picture01 / Encoder contract02 / Hashing choices03 / Delegating hashes04 / Crypto utilitiesQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 4, “Managing passwords” (book pp. 68–82). Figures come from the supplied PDF; Java examples are newly written for this guide.
The 60-second takeaway

Store a password hash, not a recoverable password.

The authentication provider uses a PasswordEncoder to check a submitted password against the stored representation. Spring Security provides password hashers and a delegating encoder for mixed formats. Its crypto module also offers key generators and encryptors—but reversible encryption serves a different purpose.

01

The PasswordEncoder contract

The chapter’s central interface connects two operations: encode(raw) creates the stored representation, and matches(raw, encoded) checks a login attempt against it. They must agree on the format. A third method, upgradeEncoding(encoded), signals that a stored value should be upgraded when your authentication flow has the raw password available.

At account creation

Encode once

Hash the chosen password with a suitable password encoder, then store only the encoded result.

raw → stored hash
At sign-in

Match, don’t decrypt

Compare the submitted raw password with the stored hash through the same compatible encoder.

raw + hash → true / false
Do not copy the insecure teaching examples. The book illustrates the contract with plaintext and unsalted SHA-512 implementations. Neither is a suitable choice for storing real passwords: use a purpose-built, slow, salted password hashing algorithm instead.
02

Choose a password hasher

Spring Security includes BCryptPasswordEncoder, Pbkdf2PasswordEncoder, and SCryptPasswordEncoder. Their work factors and resource costs can be tuned. NoOpPasswordEncoder does nothing and StandardPasswordEncoder is deprecated; neither belongs in a new production design.

B

BCrypt

A slow password hash with a configurable work factor; a practical default for many applications.

P

PBKDF2

Derives a password hash using repeated work; iterations and algorithm settings affect cost.

S

SCrypt

Includes tunable CPU and memory costs, parallelization, key length, and salt length.

The following standalone demo uses Spring Security’s delegating encoder, which writes new hashes with a {bcrypt} prefix. It reads a local test password from an environment variable so the example does not put a secret in source code. Use the security starter from chapter 2 (or the spring-security-crypto dependency).

PasswordDemo.java · encode and verify
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.factory.PasswordEncoderFactories;

public class PasswordDemo {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    String raw = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (raw == null || raw.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for the local demo");
    }

    PasswordEncoder encoder = PasswordEncoderFactories
        .createDelegatingPasswordEncoder();
    String storedHash = encoder.encode(raw);
    boolean valid = encoder.matches(raw, storedHash);

    System.out.println(storedHash.startsWith("{bcrypt}"));
    System.out.println(valid); // true: the input matches the stored hash
  }
}

In a real login, raw is the password submitted by the user, while storedHash is retrieved from persistent storage. Do not log either value in production. The chapter 3 UserManagementConfig can use the same encoder by replacing its passwordEncoder() bean with PasswordEncoderFactories.createDelegatingPasswordEncoder().

03

One interface, multiple hash formats

DelegatingPasswordEncoder uses a prefix such as {bcrypt} to choose the corresponding verifier. That lets an application recognize stored hashes from more than one scheme while writing new passwords with its selected encoding algorithm.

Migration detail. The identifier selected for new encoding is not automatically a fallback for verifying unprefixed hashes. In Spring Security 6, an unmapped or missing prefix normally fails matching unless you explicitly configure a suitable legacy fallback. Plan and test migrations instead of silently accepting unknown formats.
04

Hashing is not encryption

A password hash is designed for verification, not recovery. Encryption is reversible by an authorized party holding the right key. The Spring Security Crypto module offers KeyGenerators for random key material and Encryptors for reversible byte or text encryption.

One-way

Password hashing

Use a password encoder for login credentials. The original password should not be recoverable from its stored hash.

verify, never decrypt
Reversible

Data encryption

Use an encryptor if the application must later recover a secret. Protect its key and retain the information needed to decrypt.

encrypt ↔ decrypt

The chapter introduces KeyGenerators.string() for a random salt, KeyGenerators.secureRandom(length) for random bytes, and text/byte encryptors. The following local demonstration uses Encryptors.delux(), the chapter’s GCM-based text option, rather than its CBC-based text() variant.

CryptoDemo.java · reversible encryption demo
import org.springframework.security.crypto.encrypt.Encryptors;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.encrypt.TextEncryptor;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.keygen.KeyGenerators;

public class CryptoDemo {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    String keyPassword = System.getenv("DEMO_ENCRYPTION_PASSWORD");
    if (keyPassword == null || keyPassword.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_ENCRYPTION_PASSWORD");
    }

    String salt = KeyGenerators.string().generateKey();
    TextEncryptor encryptor = Encryptors.delux(keyPassword, salt);
    String ciphertext = encryptor.encrypt("local test note");
    String plaintext = encryptor.decrypt(ciphertext);

    System.out.println(plaintext.equals("local test note"));
  }
}
SAFETYFor persistent ciphertext, keep the salt with the encrypted value and manage the encryption password/key securely across restarts (for example, using a secrets manager); never hardcode it or print plaintext. Encryption does not replace password hashing. Avoid Encryptors.noOpText() outside tests.
✓

Keep these ideas

01encode() produces a stored password hash; matches() checks submitted input.
02Prefer purpose-built password hashers, not plaintext or a fast standalone digest.
03A {bcrypt}-style prefix lets a delegating encoder select the correct verifier.
04Key generators and encryptors solve reversible-secret problems, not password storage.

Check your understanding

Why is a plain SHA-512 digest a poor password store?

It is fast and the simple version in the book does not use a per-password salt. Attackers can try many guesses quickly. Use a purpose-built password hasher such as bcrypt, PBKDF2, or scrypt with suitable parameters.

Does {bcrypt} mean the password can be decrypted?

No. It identifies the verifier for the stored hash. Matching checks a candidate input against the hash; it does not reverse it.

What must survive a restart to decrypt stored ciphertext?

The encrypted value, its salt or other required parameters, and access to the correct protected encryption key/password. Losing the key means losing the ability to decrypt.

Chapter 05 · A web app’s security begins with filters

Before the
controller.

HTTP requests pass through a chain of filters before your endpoint runs. This chapter shows how to add a check before authentication, observe a request after it, and understand why filter order matters.

Filter chain explained5 chapter figuresRunnable filter demo
A request’s route
Request validationBEFORE
Authentication filterCHECK
ControllerAFTER

The position of a filter changes what it can see.

Chapter five

The big picture01 / The chain02 / Before authentication03 / After authentication04 / Same position05 / Filter typesQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 5, “A web app’s security begins with filters” (book pp. 83–100). Selected figures are from the provided PDF; code is newly written.
The 60-second takeaway

A filter can inspect, stop, or forward a request.

Spring Security’s servlet web protection is a sequence of filters. A filter applies its own responsibility and normally calls the next filter; it can also terminate the request with a response. Place custom filters relative to known filters so they run at the right stage, and avoid assuming that sharing a position replaces an existing filter.

01

A chain of responsibilities

Like checkpoints at an airport, filters process requests in a defined sequence. Each filter may do work itself or delegate to another component; the request continues through the chain only when the filter calls filterChain.doFilter(request, response).

↘

Inspect

Read headers and request data before a protected endpoint is called.

→

Forward

Call doFilter() to continue through the chain.

×

Stop

Return an error response without forwarding when a request should be rejected.

The actual chain depends on configuration. For example, enabling HTTP Basic contributes BasicAuthenticationFilter. Spring Security also has filters for concerns such as CSRF and CORS when applicable; do not assume every filter is present in every application.

02

Run a check before authentication

Use addFilterBefore(customFilter, BasicAuthenticationFilter.class) when a rule must run before HTTP Basic authentication. In the book’s example, a missing Request-Id header stops processing with a 400 Bad Request.

The original demo below keeps authentication enabled, unlike the book’s simplified permitAll() example. Use the Chapter 2 DemoApplication.java and its web/security starters, but replace any earlier SecurityFilterChain configuration with this one—do not register competing demo chains. The default generated user applies if you have not supplied your own user service.

FilterDemoConfig.java · validation and tracing
import java.io.IOException;
import java.util.logging.Logger;
import jakarta.servlet.FilterChain;
import jakarta.servlet.ServletException;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletResponse;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.AnonymousAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.security.web.authentication.www.BasicAuthenticationFilter;
import org.springframework.web.filter.OncePerRequestFilter;

@Configuration
public class FilterDemoConfig {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain securityFilterChain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .addFilterBefore(new RequestIdFilter(), BasicAuthenticationFilter.class)
        .addFilterAfter(new AuthenticationTraceFilter(), BasicAuthenticationFilter.class)
        .build();
  }
}

class RequestIdFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
  @Override
  protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
      HttpServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    String id = request.getHeader("Request-Id");
    if (id == null || !id.matches("[A-Za-z0-9-]{1,64}")) {
      response.sendError(HttpServletResponse.SC_BAD_REQUEST, "Invalid Request-Id");
      return;
    }
    chain.doFilter(request, response);
  }
}

class AuthenticationTraceFilter extends OncePerRequestFilter {
  private static final Logger LOG =
      Logger.getLogger(AuthenticationTraceFilter.class.getName());

  @Override
  protected void doFilterInternal(HttpServletRequest request,
      HttpServletResponse response, FilterChain chain)
      throws ServletException, IOException {
    Authentication auth = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
    boolean signedIn = auth != null && auth.isAuthenticated()
        && !(auth instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken);
    LOG.info("requestId=" + request.getHeader("Request-Id")
        + " authenticated=" + signedIn);
    chain.doFilter(request, response);
  }
}
NOTEThese filters are constructed inside the security chain, not annotated as servlet @Component filters, to avoid accidental registration twice. The example validates the client-supplied ID’s format, but a client-supplied ID is not proof of identity. For trusted audit correlation, generate or verify IDs at a trusted boundary.
Terminal · local checks
# Missing ID: 400 Bad Request
curl -i http://localhost:8080/hello

# Valid ID but no credentials: 401 Unauthorized
curl -i -H "Request-Id: lesson-01" http://localhost:8080/hello

# Use the generated password from the startup log: 200 OK
curl -i -H "Request-Id: lesson-01" \
  -u "user:YOUR_GENERATED_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello
03

Observe after the Basic filter

addFilterAfter(customFilter, BasicAuthenticationFilter.class) positions a filter after the Basic authentication step. The demo’s tracing filter reads the current authentication and logs only a validated request ID and a yes/no flag, not credentials or the Authorization header.

Be precise about events. A filter positioned after the Basic filter is not a definitive audit hook for every authentication success or failure, and it runs before some later access decisions. For production security audits, use appropriate authentication/authorization events and avoid logging sensitive data.
04

Same position is not replacement

addFilterAt(customFilter, BasicAuthenticationFilter.class) places a filter at the same order slot. This is useful when implementing a different authentication approach, but it does not remove any existing filter at that slot. If both are present, execution order between them is not guaranteed.

The chapter demonstrates a static key, a signed request, and a one-time password as possible authentication inputs. Its static-header-key example is intentionally simple and weak; do not treat a hardcoded shared string or a manually checked Authorization header as a production-ready login design. Use a well-reviewed authentication mechanism and secure key storage instead.

05

Pick the simplest useful filter type

jakarta.servlet.FilterThe standard servlet contract: implement doFilter() and forward explicitly. Spring Boot 3 uses jakarta.servlet, not javax.servlet.
GenericFilterBeanA Spring base class with lifecycle/configuration conveniences; use it when those features are needed.
OncePerRequestFilterAn HTTP-oriented base class with doFilterInternal() and once-per-request-dispatch behavior. The runnable demo uses it to avoid duplicate tracing.
shouldNotFilter()Override this hook if the filter should skip certain requests; async and error dispatches have their own hooks and defaults.

A custom filter is warranted when the chain’s existing behavior does not satisfy a requirement. It should have one clear responsibility and be tested at the placement where it actually runs.

✓

Keep these ideas

01Filters run before controllers and must forward or deliberately terminate a request.
02addFilterBefore() and addFilterAfter() position custom work relative to a known filter.
03addFilterAt() shares an order slot; it does not replace another filter automatically.
04Use OncePerRequestFilter when its HTTP and dispatch behavior serves the requirement.

Check your understanding

What happens when a filter does not call doFilter()?

The request stops at that filter. It must send an appropriate response, as the validation example does with HTTP 400.

Does a filter placed after Basic prove the request was authorized?

No. It is after that authentication step, but later authorization may still deny access, and some authentication paths may not pass through Basic at all.

Why avoid two filters at the same order slot?

Spring Security does not guarantee their relative execution order. Use explicit placement and test the actual configured chain.

Chapter 06 · Implementing authentications

Who gets
in?

Chapter six brings the authentication pipeline together: a provider decides whether credentials are valid, a security context holds the result, and HTTP Basic or a login form handles the web experience.

Custom provider7 chapter figuresContext & login demos
The authentication decision
Credentials arriveREQUEST
Provider verifiesDECIDE
Security contextRESULT

Authentication establishes identity; authorization comes next.

Chapter six

The big picture01 / Provider contract02 / Custom provider03 / Security context04 / Async work05 / Basic vs. formQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 6, “Implementing authentications” (book pp. 101–134). Selected figures come from the supplied PDF; examples are original adaptations.
The 60-second takeaway

Authenticate first. Authorize second.

An AuthenticationProvider checks an authentication request and returns a trusted Authentication or fails. On success, Spring Security makes that identity available through the SecurityContext. The way the client presents credentials—HTTP Basic or a login form—is a separate choice from how those credentials are validated.

01

Represent the request; make the decision

An Authentication object represents the principal, credentials, details, authorities, and whether authentication has completed. The authentication manager delegates the decision to a provider that supports that authentication type.

supports(type)Says whether a provider understands that kind of Authentication token.
authenticate(input)Returns an authenticated token, throws AuthenticationException for a rejected request, or may return null to let another provider try.
UserDetailsServiceFinds a user by name when the authentication scheme uses stored users.
PasswordEncoderChecks a submitted password against its stored hash; it does not decrypt the password.

The book explores multiple providers and the difference between not recognizing a token and rejecting its credentials. In a typical servlet app, failed authentication often yields 401 Unauthorized; a recognized, signed-in user denied access by a later authorization rule is a different problem (typically 403 Forbidden).

02

An illustrative custom provider

A custom AuthenticationProvider is an extension point when built-in authentication does not fit. This teaching example deliberately reimplements a simple username/password check so you can see the boundary—but for ordinary username/password login, prefer Spring Security’s built-in provider.

Use this file in the same package as the Chapter 2 DemoApplication.java, with its web and security starters. Replace earlier demo security configuration files rather than registering multiple competing SecurityFilterChain beans. Set DEMO_PASSWORD before starting the app.

AuthenticationDemoConfig.java · learning-only provider
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.AccountExpiredException;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.BadCredentialsException;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.CredentialsExpiredException;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.DisabledException;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.LockedException;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetails;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UsernameNotFoundException;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.AuthenticationProvider;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class AuthenticationDemoConfig {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    String secret = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (secret == null || secret.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for the local demo");
    }
    UserDetails learner = User.withUsername("learner")
        .password(encoder.encode(secret)).authorities("READ").build();
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(learner);
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http, UserDetailsService users,
      PasswordEncoder encoder) throws Exception {
    return http
        .authenticationProvider(new DemoProvider(users, encoder))
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .build();
  }
}

class DemoProvider implements AuthenticationProvider {
  private final UserDetailsService users;
  private final PasswordEncoder encoder;

  DemoProvider(UserDetailsService users, PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    this.users = users;
    this.encoder = encoder;
  }

  @Override
  public Authentication authenticate(Authentication input) {
    Object credentials = input.getCredentials();
    if (credentials == null) throw new BadCredentialsException("Invalid credentials");
    UserDetails user;
    try {
      user = users.loadUserByUsername(input.getName());
    } catch (UsernameNotFoundException ex) {
      throw new BadCredentialsException("Invalid credentials", ex);
    }
    if (!encoder.matches(credentials.toString(), user.getPassword())) {
      throw new BadCredentialsException("Invalid credentials");
    }
    if (!user.isEnabled()) throw new DisabledException("Account disabled");
    if (!user.isAccountNonLocked()) throw new LockedException("Account locked");
    if (!user.isAccountNonExpired()) throw new AccountExpiredException("Account expired");
    if (!user.isCredentialsNonExpired()) throw new CredentialsExpiredException("Credentials expired");
    return UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken
        .authenticated(user, null, user.getAuthorities());
  }

  @Override
  public boolean supports(Class<?> type) {
    return UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken.class.isAssignableFrom(type);
  }
}
SAFETYThis is an educational example, not production authentication. It checks account status and avoids putting the raw password in the successful token, but real systems also need vetted identity storage, auditing, abuse protections, credential handling, and security tests. Do not add a custom provider merely to duplicate the framework’s built-in username/password behavior.
03

Use the current security context

After successful authentication, the filter stores an Authentication in a SecurityContext. In a traditional servlet app, SecurityContextHolder uses a thread-local strategy by default, so code handling the current request can read its authenticated identity.

At an MVC endpoint, Spring can inject Authentication directly, which is simpler than reading the holder yourself. Add this controller alongside the Chapter 2 app (and one active security configuration):

IdentityController.java · current request identity
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
public class IdentityController {
  @GetMapping("/whoami")
  String whoami(Authentication authentication) {
    return "Hello, " + authentication.getName() + "!";
  }
}

With the custom-provider demo, a local Basic request with learner and DEMO_PASSWORD returns Hello, learner!. Use HTTPS when credentials leave your machine.

04

Crossing thread boundaries

The default MODE_THREADLOCAL does not carry authentication into an unrelated worker thread. The chapter also describes inheritable thread-local and global strategies, but sharing a global context across users is inappropriate for ordinary web apps, and pooled threads make inherited context easy to mishandle.

For tasks you submit yourself, decorate the task or the executor. The following is a pattern fragment, not a standalone program: pool is an application-managed executor and the code runs while a request’s security context exists.

Task fragment · explicit context propagation
Callable<String> task = () ->
    SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication().getName();

Future<String> result = pool.submit(
    new DelegatingSecurityContextCallable<>(task));
// Or decorate a reusable pool with DelegatingSecurityContextExecutorService.
Thread-pool caution. Avoid a global context or casually inheriting a parent thread’s context in a pooled web server. Propagate the right context per task and let the security wrapper restore/clear it; do not keep one user’s identity attached to a reusable thread. This section concerns servlet/thread-local security, not reactive applications.
05

HTTP Basic or a login form?

Request credentials

HTTP Basic

The client sends credentials in a header on each request. Configure httpBasic(); a failed attempt can return a 401 challenge with a realm. Use HTTPS.

Useful for small demos and select clients
Interactive browser

Form login

Unauthenticated browser requests redirect to a generated login page; a successful login can return the user to the originally requested page.

Session-oriented web flow

To try the form flow, use this as an alternative security configuration in the Chapter 2 app—remove the custom-provider or other earlier chain first. With no custom user service, sign in using user and the password printed at startup. Open /hello in a browser; after signing in, it displays the existing endpoint response.

FormLoginConfig.java · alternative browser flow
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class FormLoginConfig {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .build();
  }
}

For HTTP Basic, the corresponding configuration uses .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults()) instead of .formLogin(...); a realm or an AuthenticationEntryPoint can tailor 401 responses. Do not disclose internal errors to the client. The form demo keeps CSRF protection enabled; real deployments also need HTTPS and a real user store.

✓

Keep these ideas

01A provider supports a token type and either authenticates it, declines it, or rejects it.
02After success, the security context holds the authenticated identity for the current request.
03New worker threads need explicit, careful security-context propagation.
04Basic and form login differ in client experience; both still rely on a trustworthy authentication decision.

Check your understanding

What is the difference between supports() and authenticate()?

supports() declares which token types the provider can process. authenticate() evaluates an actual request and returns a trusted result, declines, or throws an authentication exception.

Why can a new executor thread see no current user?

The default servlet security context is thread-local. A task on another thread does not automatically inherit the request’s context; use an appropriate delegating task or executor.

When does a browser get the generated login page?

When form login is configured and an unauthenticated browser requests a protected resource. After successful login, it can return to that resource.

Chapter 07 · Endpoint-level authorization

Access is
earned.

Knowing who called is only the first question. Chapter seven introduces the second: is that caller allowed to reach this resource? Explore authorities, roles, and rules that apply to all endpoints.

401 vs. 4037 original figuresCopyable Java examples
Two separate decisions
Who are you?AUTHENTICATE
Are you allowed?AUTHORIZE
Run the endpointALLOW

Being signed in is not permission to do everything.

Chapter seven

The big picture01 / After login02 / Authorities03 / Roles04 / Complex rules05 / Permit or denyQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 7, “Configuring endpoint-level authorization: Restricting access” (book pp. 137–155). Figures are embedded from the supplied PDF; Java examples are original adaptations.
The 60-second takeaway

Identity does not equal permission.

Authentication identifies the requester. Authorization evaluates a rule against that identity and the requested action. This chapter applies rules with anyRequest()—the same restriction for every endpoint. Chapter 8 will show how to select particular paths and methods.

01

Authorization follows authentication

Even a well-known user may lack permission for a particular resource. After authentication, Spring Security makes the user’s identity and authorities available in the security context; the authorization step decides whether the request continues to the controller.

Not signed in

Typically 401

The request has not established an authenticated identity. The app can challenge the client to authenticate.

Who are you?
Signed in, not allowed

Typically 403

Authentication succeeded, but the caller does not satisfy the access rule.

You cannot do this.
02

Grant precise authorities

A user’s UserDetails carries a collection of GrantedAuthority values. An authority is a named privilege such as READ or WRITE. The configured rule checks the exact name; be consistent about spelling and case.

1

hasAuthority()

Require one exact authority, such as WRITE.

∨

hasAnyAuthority()

Permit a caller with at least one of several named authorities.

ƒ

access()

Supply an AuthorizationManager for rules that need more than the simpler helpers.

This self-contained teaching configuration works with DemoApplication.java and the web/security starters from chapter 2. Replace earlier demo security configurations; do not run multiple competing chains. Set DEMO_PASSWORD locally before starting it. The example uses BCrypt instead of the book’s plaintext-password shortcut.

AuthorizationDemoConfig.java · all endpoints require WRITE
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
public class AuthorizationDemoConfig {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    String secret = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (secret == null || secret.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for the local demo");
    }
    var john = User.withUsername("john")
        .password(encoder.encode(secret)).authorities("READ").build();
    var jane = User.withUsername("jane")
        .password(encoder.encode(secret)).authorities("WRITE").build();
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(john, jane);
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().hasAuthority("WRITE"))
        .build();
  }
}
Terminal · compare the two users locally
# No credentials: usually 401 Unauthorized
curl -i http://localhost:8080/hello

# John has READ, not WRITE: 403 Forbidden
curl -i -u "john:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello

# Jane has WRITE: 200 OK, Hello!
curl -i -u "jane:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello
NOTEHTTP Basic is only suitable over HTTPS when traffic is not strictly local. The shared demo secret and in-memory accounts are teaching conveniences, not production identity management. The chapter’s anyRequest() rule applies to every route, including any extra endpoints you add.
03

Use roles for broader labels

A role is a coarse-grained label such as ADMIN or MANAGER. Spring Security represents it as a granted authority with the ROLE_ prefix. roles("ADMIN") creates ROLE_ADMIN; hasRole("ADMIN") checks for it. Do not include the prefix in either method’s argument.

Role variant · fragment, not an additional bean
// In a UserDetailsService bean, build a role-bearing user:
var admin = User.withUsername("admin")
    .password(encoder.encode(secret))
    .roles("ADMIN")      // stores ROLE_ADMIN
    .build();

// In the SecurityFilterChain, use this instead of hasAuthority("WRITE"):
.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().hasRole("ADMIN"))
Role is not a permission bundle by magic. roles("ADMIN") grants ROLE_ADMIN; it does not automatically grant separate READ, WRITE, or DELETE authorities. If your design needs those privileges, assign them explicitly or configure and test an appropriate role hierarchy.
04

Reach for complex rules sparingly

When a single authority or role check cannot express the requirement, access() accepts an AuthorizationManager. The chapter uses WebExpressionAuthorizationManager to express “has READ but not DELETE.” Prefer the small helpers for simple policies—they are easier to audit.

Expression variant · fragment, not an additional bean
import org.springframework.security.web.access.expression.WebExpressionAuthorizationManager;

// Inside authorizeHttpRequests(...), instead of hasAuthority("WRITE"):
auth.anyRequest().access(new WebExpressionAuthorizationManager(
    "hasAuthority('READ') and !hasAuthority('DELETE')"));

This fragment requires users and authorities consistent with the expression. In the chapter’s example, a reader with only READ is permitted, while a user who also has DELETE is rejected. Do not take arbitrary untrusted input and turn it into a security expression.

05

Permit all, deny all, or decide

permitAll() accepts matching requests without requiring a login. denyAll() rejects matching requests regardless of their identity. In this chapter, pairing either with anyRequest() applies the rule everywhere; the next chapter explains how to target specific requests.

Open by intent

permitAll()

Use only for routes that are meant to be public; avoid accidentally opening unrelated endpoints.

Closed by intent

denyAll()

A safe fallback when a service must reject requests outside its responsibility.

✓

Keep these ideas

01Authorization checks permission after a caller has been identified.
02hasAuthority() checks one exact privilege; hasAnyAuthority() accepts any listed privilege.
03A role is a ROLE_-prefixed authority; hasRole("ADMIN") checks ROLE_ADMIN.
04Use access() for complex policies, and denyAll() for intentional rejection.

Check your understanding

Why does John receive 403 while Jane receives 200 in the demo?

Both have valid credentials, but the rule requires WRITE. Jane has that authority; John has only READ.

Does roles("ADMIN") add READ automatically?

No. It adds the single granted authority ROLE_ADMIN. Extra privileges require explicit modeling or a tested role hierarchy.

What does anyRequest() mean in this chapter?

The same authorization rule applies to every incoming request. Chapter 8 introduces request matching to apply different rules to different paths or methods.

Chapter 08 · Applying endpoint restrictions

Match the
request.

Chapter seven defined who is allowed. Chapter eight adds where and when a rule applies: match the path, optionally match the HTTP method, then choose a clear fallback for everything else.

Path & method rules3 embedded visualsCopyable Java examples
The matcher pipeline
GET /helloREQUEST
Match path + methodSELECT
Check the ruleDECIDE

The first matching authorization rule wins.

Chapter eight

The big picture01 / Different routes02 / Rule order03 / Path & method04 / Regex fallbackQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 8, “Configuring endpoint-level authorization: Applying restrictions” (book pp. 156–174). The chapter has one numbered figure; the two other diagrams here are newly drawn inline SVGs.
The 60-second takeaway

One application, different access rules.

requestMatchers() selects which requests a rule governs. Match an exact route, a path pattern, an HTTP method plus path, or—only when simpler patterns cannot express the requirement—a regular expression. Put specific rules first and finish with an explicit anyRequest() policy.

01

Assign rules to routes

Chapter 7 applied the same rule everywhere with anyRequest(). Here, requestMatchers("/hello") can require the ADMIN role while requestMatchers("/ciao") requires MANAGER. A public health endpoint can have its own rule.

The following standalone learning configuration works with the Chapter 2 web/security starters. It includes its own endpoints and two in-memory users with BCrypt-hashed passwords. Add it alongside DemoApplication.java, but remove earlier demo controllers/configurations that would duplicate paths or define competing filter chains. Set DEMO_PASSWORD for local testing.

RouteRulesConfig.java · runnable route rules
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@Configuration
public class RouteRulesConfig {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    String secret = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (secret == null || secret.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for the local demo");
    }
    var john = User.withUsername("john")
        .password(encoder.encode(secret)).roles("ADMIN").build();
    var jane = User.withUsername("jane")
        .password(encoder.encode(secret)).roles("MANAGER").build();
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(john, jane);
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers("/hello").hasRole("ADMIN")
            .requestMatchers("/ciao").hasRole("MANAGER")
            .requestMatchers("/health").permitAll()
            .anyRequest().denyAll())
        .build();
  }
}

@RestController
class RouteController {
  @GetMapping("/hello")
  String hello() { return "Hello!"; }

  @GetMapping("/ciao")
  String ciao() { return "Ciao!"; }

  @GetMapping("/health")
  String health() { return "OK"; }
}
Terminal · local behavior
# Public route: 200 OK
curl -i http://localhost:8080/health

# Wrong role: 403 Forbidden
curl -i -u "jane:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello

# Correct roles: 200 OK
curl -i -u "john:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello
curl -i -u "jane:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/ciao

# Credentials are still checked on a public route: bad Basic auth → 401
curl -i -u "jane:wrong" http://localhost:8080/health
NOTEPublic permitAll() is an authorization decision, not a promise to ignore an invalid Authorization header. A malformed or wrong Basic credential can fail authentication before the public route is reached. Use HTTP Basic only over HTTPS outside a strictly local demo.
02

Specific rules before the fallback

Authorization matchers are evaluated in the order written; the first match supplies the policy. Put exact and narrower rules before broad patterns. Finish with anyRequest().authenticated() or anyRequest().denyAll() rather than leaving unmatched paths ambiguous.

Intentional public access

permitAll()

A path is reachable without logging in, such as the small demo’s /health.

Explicit fallback

denyAll()

Everything not deliberately listed is blocked. This avoids accidentally opening a newly added endpoint.

Ordering trap. A broad "/a/**" matcher placed before a narrow "/a/b" matcher can absorb that path first. anyRequest() belongs last, after all specific rules.
03

Match path and HTTP method

requestMatchers("/a/b") selects a path without choosing an HTTP method. requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/a") selects both method and path. Patterns let several related endpoints share a rule; the exact syntax can depend on the matcher implementation selected by your Spring Security/MVC setup.

/aAn exact path rule.
/a/*One additional path segment, such as /a/b.
/a/**A path prefix and nested descendants, such as /a/b/c.
/product/{code:[0-9]+}A path variable constrained to one or more digits when MVC path-variable regex matching is available.
Method + path · replace the route rules in a separate demo
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;

// Inside authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth ...):
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/reports/**").hasAuthority("READ")
.requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/reports").hasAuthority("WRITE")
.anyRequest().denyAll()
CSRFThe book temporarily disables CSRF to demonstrate unauthenticated POST requests. This guide does not disable it. A state-changing request can be rejected for a missing CSRF token even when its authorization rule would otherwise allow it; chapter 9 explains CSRF protection. Do not publish an unauthenticated state-changing endpoint just to test a matcher.
04

Use regex only when needed

For unusually complex paths, requestMatchers(new RegexRequestMatcher(...)) can select requests by a regular expression. Regex is powerful, but often harder to read and audit than a path pattern. Keep patterns narrow, test allowed and denied cases, and avoid using regex as a substitute for business validation.

The chapter’s example grants authenticated users access to some country/language video paths and requires a premium authority for others. An illustrative modern matcher fragment is below. Use it as an alternative rule set in a separate app with matching endpoints/users, not as a second filter chain.

Regex matcher · optional advanced fragment
import org.springframework.security.web.util.matcher.RegexRequestMatcher;

// Inside authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth ...):
.requestMatchers(new RegexRequestMatcher(
    "^/video/(us|uk|ca)/(en|fr)(\\?.*)?$", "GET"))
    .authenticated()
.requestMatchers("/video/**").hasAuthority("PREMIUM")
.anyRequest().denyAll()

The optional query-string part makes the pattern usable when query parameters are present. The narrow regex must appear before the broader /video/** rule. This selects requests; it does not validate country or language input for other purposes.

✓

Keep these ideas

01requestMatchers() selects the path and optionally the HTTP method for an access rule.
02Order rules from specific to general; make the anyRequest() fallback explicit.
03A public route does not make bad supplied credentials valid, and CSRF is a separate check.
04Use path expressions first; reserve full regex matchers for requirements they cannot express.

Check your understanding

Which rule wins if /a/** appears before /a/b?

The broad rule can match /a/b first. Put the more specific path before the broader one.

Can a public route still return 401?

Yes. If a request supplies invalid HTTP Basic credentials, authentication can fail before the permitAll() authorization rule is evaluated.

Why might a POST return 403 even with a matching access rule?

CSRF protection is separate from authorization. Without a valid CSRF token in a session-based setup, Spring Security may reject a state-changing request; chapter 9 covers this mechanism.
