Chapter 09 · Configuring CSRF protection

Trust the
intent.

A logged-in browser can be tricked into sending a request. CSRF protection asks for a second proof—one the attacker’s page cannot simply supply—before the server accepts a state-changing action.

Threat & token11 book figuresForms & customization
The two-request handshake
GET pageREAD
Page receives tokenPROOF
POST + tokenCHANGE

No valid token? The unsafe request is rejected.

Chapter nine

The big picture01 / The attack02 / Filter & token03 / Working forms04 / Exceptions05 / Token storageQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 9, “Configuring CSRF protection” (book pp. 175–198). All eleven numbered book figures are reproduced from the supplied PDF. Demo code is newly written; production caveats are called out separately.
The 60-second takeaway

Authentication alone cannot prove who initiated a browser request.

When a browser automatically sends a session cookie, another site may try to cause a state-changing request on the user’s behalf. Spring Security enables CSRF protection by default: its filter generally lets safe methods through but requires a valid token for unsafe methods. Keep it enabled for cookie-authenticated web apps; include a token in your own POST forms and deliberate exceptions only after a threat-model review.

01

The browser is the unwitting messenger

Imagine Carlos is signed in to his company’s account-management site. He opens a separate music site that contains attacker-controlled markup. That page induces his browser to send a request to the company site; if the company site trusts only the automatically attached login cookie, Carlos’s accounts can be changed without his intent.

What the attack exploits

Ambient credentials

The browser may attach the target site’s cookies even when another page initiates the request. The attacker need not know the password.

What the defense tests

A separate token

For a state-changing request, the target expects a value obtained through its own pages or API, bound to the user’s session or equivalent state.

Do not mutate on GET. Safe methods such as GET are not required to carry a CSRF token by the default rule. Never use a GET endpoint to delete, buy, transfer, or otherwise change application state. Browsers, crawlers, and prefetchers may invoke GET without a user’s explicit intent.
02

How the filter checks the token

CsrfFilter sits in the Spring Security filter chain. By default, it does not require a token for GET, HEAD, TRACE, or OPTIONS; for POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE, and other unsafe methods, it compares the submitted value with the expected one. Missing or invalid token → 403 Forbidden, independently of whether the authorization rule would otherwise grant access.

In the chapter’s first exercise, a temporary CsrfTokenLogger reads the _csrf request attribute after CsrfFilter, then copies the token from a log into a POST header. It demonstrates where the token lives; logging it would expose a secret in a real system. The default repository stores the expected token in the HTTP session. Modern Spring Security can defer loading the token until it is accessed, so a safe GET need not always materialize a new value.

CsrfTokenHolds the token value and its HTTP header and form-parameter names.
CsrfTokenRepositoryGenerates, saves, and loads the expected value (session-backed by default).
CsrfTokenRequestHandlerExposes and resolves token values on requests; modern defaults may mask tokens in rendered output.
CsrfFilterApplies the matcher and rejects unsafe requests without a valid submitted token.
03

Make a POST form work

The chapter’s next experiment uses Spring MVC, form login, and Thymeleaf. Spring Security’s generated login page already includes a hidden token. A hand-written form that posts a product without a token receives 403; add a hidden field containing ${_csrf.token}, named ${_csrf.parameterName}, and submit with the same browser session.

Try this separate teaching app with the Spring Boot web, security, and Thymeleaf starters. Put the Java class in your application package (add the matching package declaration if needed) and the template at src/main/resources/templates/main.html. Avoid mixing it with the previous chapter’s competing controller and filter-chain demos. Set DEMO_PASSWORD before starting; do not use this in-memory login arrangement as a production identity system.

CsrfFormsDemo.java · one-file teaching configuration
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Controller;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RequestParam;

@Configuration
public class CsrfFormsDemo {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    String secret = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (secret == null || secret.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for local testing");
    }
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(User.withUsername("mary")
        .password(encoder.encode(secret)).roles("USER").build());
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .formLogin(form -> form.defaultSuccessUrl("/main", true).permitAll())
        .build(); // CSRF stays enabled
  }
}

@Controller
class MainPageController {
  @GetMapping("/main")
  String main() { return "main"; }

  @PostMapping("/product/add")
  String add(@RequestParam String name) {
    // Teaching stub: validate and persist in a real application.
    return "redirect:/main";
  }
}
templates/main.html · Thymeleaf form
<!doctype html>
<html lang="en" xmlns:th="http://www.thymeleaf.org">
<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Products</title></head>
<body>
  <h1>Add a product</h1>
  <form action="/product/add" method="post">
    <label>Name <input name="name" required></label>
    <input type="hidden" th:name="${_csrf.parameterName}"
                         th:value="${_csrf.token}">
    <button type="submit">Add</button>
  </form>
</body>
</html>

Open /main in a browser, sign in as mary, and submit the form. To reproduce the failure first, temporarily remove the hidden input only and submit again: expect 403. Restore it for a successful POST and redirect. The plain action attribute above avoids relying on template-engine automatic CSRF field insertion; some Thymeleaf/Spring integrations inject a field when using th:action, so do not submit duplicate token fields.

BoundaryCSRF protects against forged browser requests; it does not authorize a user, prevent XSS, or replace input validation. SameSite cookies and CORS have different roles; CORS alone is not a CSRF defense. Evaluate cookie-authenticated SPAs and non-browser clients by how credentials and tokens are actually transmitted, not by the label “REST API.”
04

Narrow exceptions, not a global off switch

The chapter allows one POST path, /ciao, to bypass CSRF while /hello remains protected. Configure csrf.ignoringRequestMatchers(...) with a path or an explicit RequestMatcher. This is not the same as authorizeHttpRequests(...).permitAll(): one controls the token check, the other controls who may access the endpoint.

CSRF exception · optional fragment, not part of the form demo
// Inside your SecurityFilterChain configuration:
http.csrf(csrf -> csrf
    .ignoringRequestMatchers("/ciao"));
// Other unsafe paths still require a CSRF token.
Threat-model first. Exempt a state-changing path only when it does not rely on automatically attached browser credentials (or another appropriate defense prevents forgery). A public or webhook endpoint may need signature verification and rate limiting; simply ignoring CSRF never makes it secure. Prefer precise method/path matchers where possible.
05

Customize where tokens live

The default HttpSessionCsrfTokenRepository keeps the expected value in the session. The chapter’s advanced exercise implements CsrfTokenRepository to persist tokens in a database, keyed by an illustrative client identifier. Its Spring Data repository sits behind the CSRF token repository; the filter does not speak to the database directly.

generateToken(request)Create a new unpredictable value, e.g., a UUID wrapped in DefaultCsrfToken("X-CSRF-TOKEN", "_csrf", value).
saveToken(token, request, response)Persist or remove the expected value for the correct session/client context; handle null tokens and rotation.
loadToken(request)Look up the expected value for that context and return a CsrfToken, or null when none exists.

The chapter sets a CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler alongside its repository for a simpler token flow. Modern Spring Security’s default XorCsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler masks values exposed to views to mitigate BREACH-style compression attacks; choosing the simpler handler changes those properties. Do not copy the example’s client-supplied X-IDENTIFIER as a trusted user identity: it is merely a pedagogical placeholder and could let one client select another client’s token record. A production implementation needs an authenticated, tamper-resistant binding, safe token lifecycle, and storage/access controls. Moving only CSRF tokens to a database does not make session-based login stateless.

Token strategy · conceptual wiring, requires a real repository
// Inside your SecurityFilterChain configuration;
// customRepository must implement CsrfTokenRepository.
http.csrf(csrf -> csrf
    .csrfTokenRepository(customRepository)
    .csrfTokenRequestHandler(
        new CsrfTokenRequestAttributeHandler()));
// The simpler handler mirrors the book's exercise; assess
// masking and frontend interoperability before using it.
✓

Keep these ideas

01CSRF attacks exploit a browser’s automatic credentials, not a stolen password.
02The filter checks unsafe methods for a submitted token; missing or invalid → 403.
03Include _csrf in custom POST forms; leave GET read-only.
04Scope exclusions narrowly and bind any custom repository to a trustworthy user/session context.

Check your understanding

Why does the default login form submit successfully with CSRF enabled?

Spring Security’s generated login form includes a CSRF hidden input, so the POST carries the expected value.

Will permitAll() allow a tokenless POST by itself?

No. Authorization and CSRF validation are separate checks. A publicly accessible route can still receive 403 for a missing CSRF token.

Is CSRF protection always unnecessary for an API?

No. Assess whether a browser sends credentials automatically (for example, session cookies). An API used by a cookie-authenticated browser can still be vulnerable; a non-browser client using only explicit authorization headers has a different threat model.

Chapter 10 · Configuring CORS

Cross the
boundary.

A page and an API can live at different origins. CORS tells a browser when code from one origin may read responses from another—without replacing authentication, authorization, or CSRF protection.

Origins & headersPreflight requests4 book figures
The browser’s decision
app.example.comPAGE
api.example.comAPI
Check CORS responseBROWSER

CORS grants browser access to a response, not API permission.

Chapter ten

The big picture01 / What is an origin?02 / Response headers03 / Preflight04 / @CrossOrigin05 / Central policyQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 10, “Configuring CORS” (book pp. 199–208). Figures 10.1–10.4 come from the supplied PDF. Corrections to the book’s iframe and header shorthand are marked explicitly.
The 60-second takeaway

CORS is a browser-controlled read permission.

When JavaScript on https://app.example.com calls https://api.example.com, the request crosses an origin boundary. The API can opt in with CORS response headers. For some requests, the browser first asks permission with an OPTIONS preflight. Configure CORS narrowly, and keep your normal security controls in place.

01

An origin is a three-part address

An origin comprises scheme + host + port. Changing any part makes a different origin: https://app.example.com is not https://api.example.com, and even two ports on the same host count as different origins. The browser’s same-origin policy ordinarily prevents cross-origin JavaScript from reading the result unless the server authorizes that origin through CORS.

Same origin

Same scheme, host, port

https://app.example.com/page → https://app.example.com/api. Different paths alone do not trigger CORS.

Cross origin

Any part differs

https://app.example.com → https://api.example.com. The browser evaluates the API’s CORS policy.

This matters especially when a frontend and backend are deployed separately. A terminal client such as curl is not subject to the browser’s CORS enforcement; it can still call a reachable API. CORS is therefore not a replacement for checking who can call an endpoint.

02

The API answers with headers

The browser sends an Origin request header. If the API permits it, the response includes Access-Control-Allow-Origin with that single allowed origin (or * for an intentionally public, non-credentialed response). Preflight responses can additionally list permitted methods and request headers.

Access-Control-Allow-OriginWhich one request origin may read this response; the value is one origin or *, never a comma-separated list.
Access-Control-Allow-MethodsMethods approved for a browser’s preflight, such as GET or POST.
Access-Control-Allow-HeadersRequest headers approved for a preflight, such as Content-Type or a custom header.
Access-Control-Allow-CredentialsWhether credentialed cross-origin requests may expose their response; requires an explicit origin, not *.
Book correctionFigures 10.2–10.3 use an iframe to explain cross-origin communication. Browsers usually can display cross-origin iframes; the same-origin policy stops parent scripts from reading the iframe’s document. Iframe embedding is controlled separately by CSP frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options. Likewise, Access-Control-Allow-Origin: example.com, example.org is illustrative, not a valid multi-origin response. Configure a list on the server; it emits one allowed origin for a matching request (often with Vary: Origin). Use complete origins including scheme.
Credentials are a separate choice. Cross-origin fetch() does not send cookies by default. If your application deliberately uses cookies across origins, the client must opt in, the server must allow credentials with an explicit allowed origin, and cookie policies (for example, SameSite/Secure) must also permit them. Keep CSRF protection for cookie-authenticated unsafe requests; CORS does not replace it.
03

Some requests ask first

For a simple cross-origin request, the browser sends the actual request, then decides whether its response can be read. That means a server-side action may already have run even if the browser reports a CORS error. Other requests—such as a request with a custom header or a JSON POST—cause an OPTIONS preflight. The browser sends the actual request only if the preflight succeeds.

01 / ProbeBrowser sends OPTIONS with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method (and, when relevant, Access-Control-Request-Headers).
02 / DecideThe CORS handler checks the configured origin, method, and headers, then returns the relevant Access-Control-Allow-* headers.
03 / ActOnly after an accepted preflight does the browser send the actual request. Authentication and CSRF rules for that request still apply.

The book’s local experiment POSTs from a page loaded at localhost to 127.0.0.1. Those hostnames refer to the same machine but count as different origins. Its simple POST reaches the controller, yet the browser hides the response without CORS headers. The book temporarily disables CSRF for this isolated experiment; the safer GET-only example below leaves CSRF enabled.

04

Allow one endpoint with @CrossOrigin

For a small exception, put @CrossOrigin on a controller method (or its class). The book adds it to its /test endpoint to allow the page origin. Use a fully qualified origin—scheme, hostname, and port where applicable—and constrain methods as needed.

Endpoint-level policy · alternative to central configuration
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.CrossOrigin;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
class ReportEndpoint {
  @CrossOrigin(origins = "https://app.example.com")
  @GetMapping("/api/report")
  String report() { return "Ready"; }
}

This annotation is readable when only a few routes need cross-origin access. For many controllers it is easy to repeat a setting or forget a new endpoint. In a Spring Security application, ensure CORS is processed before security rejects preflight; configure http.cors(...) and a compatible MVC or CorsConfigurationSource policy. The central example below shows the latter. Treat the annotation and central example as alternatives, not two policies to paste into one demo.

05

Keep the policy in one place

Spring Security’s cors() support can use a CorsConfigurationSource. Give it a specific path pattern, a list of trusted origins, allowed methods, and allowed request headers. The following independent teaching configuration uses Spring Boot’s web and security starters, a public GET endpoint, and a deliberately narrow browser policy. It does not turn CSRF off.

CorsDemoConfig.java · standalone central CORS example
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import org.springframework.web.cors.CorsConfiguration;
import org.springframework.web.cors.CorsConfigurationSource;
import org.springframework.web.cors.UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource;

@Configuration
public class CorsDemoConfig {
  @Bean
  CorsConfigurationSource corsConfigurationSource() {
    CorsConfiguration policy = new CorsConfiguration();
    policy.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://app.example.com"));
    policy.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET"));
    policy.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("X-Client-Id"));
    UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource source =
        new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
    source.registerCorsConfiguration("/api/**", policy);
    return source;
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().permitAll())
        .build(); // CSRF remains enabled for unsafe methods
  }
}

@RestController
class ReportController {
  @GetMapping("/api/report")
  String report() { return "Ready"; }
}

Add the class to your Spring Boot application package (and add its matching package declaration). Do not include the separate annotation example’s controller in the same app: it defines the same path. The production frontend origin here is illustrative; curl can simulate that origin locally, but a real browser test needs a page actually served from that origin. In production, keep CORS policy for this public endpoint only as broad as your data exposure permits; authorization is a separate decision.

Terminal · inspect CORS headers locally (curl is not a browser)
# Allowed origin: response includes Access-Control-Allow-Origin
curl -i -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' \
  http://localhost:8080/api/report

# Simulate a browser's preflight for GET with a custom header
curl -i -X OPTIONS \
  -H 'Origin: https://app.example.com' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Method: GET' \
  -H 'Access-Control-Request-Headers: X-Client-Id' \
  http://localhost:8080/api/report

# An unlisted origin should not receive permission to read the response
curl -i -H 'Origin: https://other.example.com' \
  http://localhost:8080/api/report
Remembercurl prints responses whether or not CORS headers allow a browser page to read them. The book’s central configuration disables CSRF solely to simplify its POST demo; this GET-only example does not. If you later add credentialed or state-changing routes, configure authentication, CSRF, cookies, and CORS together. A permissive CORS policy is not itself XSS or DDoS protection or a defense against non-browser callers.
✓

Keep these ideas

01Origins compare scheme, host, and port—not just domain names.
02The server declares permission, but the browser enforces access to cross-origin responses.
03A preflight asks before some requests; a simple request may reach the server even if its response is blocked.
04Use @CrossOrigin for small cases or a centralized CorsConfigurationSource for shared policy; keep auth and CSRF separate.

Check your understanding

Why is localhost:8080 different from localhost:3000?

Different ports mean different origins, even when scheme and host are identical.

If the browser displays a CORS error, did the server definitely reject the request?

No. A simple request can reach the server and run its handler; the browser may merely hide the response from the calling page. A failed preflight, on the other hand, prevents the browser from sending the subsequent actual request.

Can CORS permit several origins by returning a comma-separated Access-Control-Allow-Origin?

No. Configure multiple origins server-side, then respond with one matching origin per request (or * only where appropriate for non-credentialed requests).

The chapter’s iframe and comma-separated-origin depictions are retained as book artwork but corrected in adjacent text; its temporarily CSRF-disabled demonstration is replaced with a GET-only, CSRF-enabled example.

Chapter 11 · Method-level authorization

Protect the
action.

An endpoint rule protects an HTTP path. Method security protects the operation itself—wherever a Spring-managed caller reaches it—and can make decisions from arguments or returned objects.

Pre & post checksPermissions7 book figures
The protected call
ControllerCALLER
Security interceptorRULE
Service methodACTION

Decide before execution—or inspect the result afterward.

Chapter eleven

The big picture01 / Enable security02 / Preauthorize03 / Arguments04 / Postauthorize05 / Permissions06 / Other annotationsQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 11, “Implementing authorization at the method level” (book pp. 209–234). All seven numbered figures are embedded from the supplied PDF. The runnable demo uses BCrypt instead of the book’s NoOp encoder.
The 60-second takeaway

Place the rule next to the behavior it protects.

Enable method security with @EnableMethodSecurity. Put @PreAuthorize on a Spring-managed method to decide before it runs, using the caller’s authorities or method arguments. Use @PostAuthorize when the rule needs the returned object—but remember the operation already executed. For richer rules, delegate hasPermission(...) to a permission evaluator. Chapter 12 will cover filtering inputs and outputs.

01

Enable the method boundary

Chapter 8 authorized requests by path. A service method can also be called by several controllers—or from outside HTTP altogether. Method security applies the rule at the selected application layer, rather than repeating it in every route that reaches that layer.

Method authorization is disabled until you opt in. Put @EnableMethodSecurity on a configuration class; pre/post annotations then work without extra switches. Spring Security intercepts calls through Spring AOP, checks the rule, and either proceeds or throws AccessDeniedException. In an HTTP app that exception typically becomes 403 for an authenticated caller; in a non-web app, your caller handles the exception.

Proxy trapIn the usual Spring AOP setup, calling a secured method from another method on the same instance bypasses the proxy. An object created manually with new is not secured by Spring’s proxy either. Keep the protected service in a Spring-managed bean and call it through another bean, as in the demo below. Test the denied path, not only the successful one.
02

Preauthorize: stop the work

@PreAuthorize evaluates a Spring Expression Language (SpEL) rule before the method body runs. If it fails, the method is not invoked. The book’s NameService.getName() requires a write authority: Emma has it; Natalie does not.

Here is a self-contained teaching configuration for a Spring Boot project with the web and security starters. Put it in your application package, adding a matching package declaration; keep your existing Boot application class. Remove competing demo controllers or filter chains from earlier chapters. Set DEMO_PASSWORD locally; the users are in memory and the passwords are BCrypt-encoded.

MethodRulesDemo.java · preauthorization and argument checks
import java.util.List;
import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.method.configuration.EnableMethodSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreAuthorize;
import org.springframework.security.core.parameters.P;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PathVariable;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
public class MethodRulesDemo {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder encoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    String password = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (password == null || password.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for local testing");
    }
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(
        User.withUsername("emma").password(encoder.encode(password))
            .authorities("write").build(),
        User.withUsername("natalie").password(encoder.encode(password))
            .authorities("read").build());
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .build();
  }
}

@Service
class NameService {
  private final Map<String, List<String>> secrets = Map.of(
      "emma", List.of("Fantastico"),
      "natalie", List.of("Energico", "Perfecto"));

  @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('write')")
  public String getName() { return "Fantastico"; }

  @PreAuthorize("#name == authentication.name")
  public List<String> getSecretNames(@P("name") String name) {
    return secrets.getOrDefault(name, List.of());
  }
}

@RestController
class MethodDemoController {
  private final NameService names;
  MethodDemoController(NameService names) { this.names = names; }

  @GetMapping("/hello")
  String hello() { return "Hello, " + names.getName(); }

  @GetMapping("/secret/names/{name}")
  List<String> names(@PathVariable("name") String name) {
    return names.getSecretNames(name);
  }
}
Terminal · exercise allowed and denied calls
# Has 'write' authority: 200, Hello, Fantastico
curl -i -u "emma:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello

# Lacks 'write': 403; the service method is not invoked
curl -i -u "natalie:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello

# Own name: 200; someone else's name: 403
curl -i -u "emma:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/secret/names/emma
curl -i -u "emma:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/secret/names/natalie
03

Use arguments to enforce ownership

Preauthorization can compare a method argument with the current principal. In the demo, #name == authentication.name allows Emma to request /secret/names/emma but denies /secret/names/natalie before data retrieval. The @P("name") annotation makes that argument name discoverable by Spring Security even when the Java compiler does not preserve parameter names.

Authorization is not a user-supplied claim. Compare the requested owner to the authenticated principal, not to a username supplied by the browser in a header or query parameter. An endpoint rule may still be useful, but the method rule remains meaningful when other parts of the app call the same service.
04

Postauthorize: inspect the result

@PostAuthorize evaluates after the method returns. Its SpEL has access to returnObject, so a service can load a record and then check a property of that record before exposing it to the caller. If the rule fails, the caller gets an access-denied error, but the method has already run.

In the book, an employee object has a roles field. The condition returnObject.roles.contains('reader') checks that field, not whether the caller has a reader authority: any authenticated user can see a qualifying record in that particular example. This smaller fragment expresses the same lesson, adding a null guard.

Post-check · separate service example, not part of the runnable demo
// In a Spring-managed service with a repository that returns Employee:
@PostAuthorize("returnObject != null and returnObject.getRoles().contains('reader')")
public Employee getBookDetails(String name) {
  return repository.findByName(name);
}
// This decides whether to expose the result; it does NOT
// limit access to the caller's own employee record.
Side effectsNever depend on a post-check to prevent a state-changing operation. Writes, external calls, and other effects may already have happened; a transaction may even have committed before postauthorization fails (depending on interceptor ordering and configuration). Put a pre-check at the right boundary for mutations; use a post-check for rules that truly require the returned data.
05

Move complex rules into a permission evaluator

The book’s document rule is “admin or document owner.” Rather than embedding a long expression in the annotation, hasPermission(...) delegates to a PermissionEvaluator. Spring Security supplies the current Authentication; your evaluator receives the object (or its ID and type) and a permission label.

Object already available

After the fetch

@PostAuthorize("hasPermission(returnObject, 'read')") calls the object-based evaluator. The result was retrieved already.

Only ID available

Before the fetch

@PreAuthorize("hasPermission(#code, 'document', 'read')") calls the ID/type evaluator before the protected method executes.

This is an adaptation recipe, not a second runnable app: provide your own Document and DocumentStore (with owner() and find(String)), then register the evaluator with a method-security expression-handler bean. Both overloads deny missing documents instead of dereferencing null. A real lookup needs careful query scope and authorization tests.

PermissionEvaluator · adapt to your document store
import java.io.Serializable;
import org.springframework.security.access.PermissionEvaluator;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Component;

@Component
class DocumentPermissions implements PermissionEvaluator {
  private final DocumentStore store;
  DocumentPermissions(DocumentStore store) { this.store = store; }

  @Override
  public boolean hasPermission(Authentication user, Object target,
                               Object permission) {
    if (user == null || !(target instanceof Document doc)
        || !"read".equals(permission)) {
      return false;
    }
    return user.getAuthorities().stream()
        .anyMatch(a -> a.getAuthority().equals("ROLE_ADMIN"))
        || user.getName().equals(doc.owner());
  }

  @Override
  public boolean hasPermission(Authentication user, Serializable id,
                               String type, Object permission) {
    if (!"document".equals(type) || !(id instanceof String code)) {
      return false;
    }
    return hasPermission(user, store.find(code), permission);
  }
}
Wiring and annotations · adapt as a separate configuration
// In the @EnableMethodSecurity configuration class:
// import MethodSecurityExpressionHandler and
// DefaultMethodSecurityExpressionHandler from
// org.springframework.security.access.expression.method
@Bean
static MethodSecurityExpressionHandler expressionHandler(
    DocumentPermissions evaluator) {
  var handler = new DefaultMethodSecurityExpressionHandler();
  handler.setPermissionEvaluator(evaluator);
  return handler;
}

// Choose ONE method rule in your Spring-managed service:
@PostAuthorize("hasPermission(returnObject, 'read')")
public Document getDocument(String code) { return store.find(code); }

// OR authorize by ID before invoking the method:
// @P binds the SpEL name even without -parameters.
@PreAuthorize("hasPermission(#code, 'document', 'read')")
public Document getDocument(@P("code") String code) {
  return store.find(code);
}
Separate versions, not overloads to paste together. The two getDocument(String) examples show alternative timings and must not coexist with the same signature. For an ID-based pre-check, the evaluator itself performs a lookup before the service method; plan for that extra query or integrate a shared authorization/data-access strategy. Check that ROLE_ADMIN matches the actual stored authority; roles("ADMIN") creates this prefixed authority.
06

Other method annotations

With @EnableMethodSecurity, pre/post authorization works by default. Two simpler alternatives are opt-in: @Secured uses authorities, while Jakarta’s @RolesAllowed names roles. Neither accepts the flexible SpEL conditions that pre/post annotations do.

Alternative annotations · separate example, not combined with the demo
@EnableMethodSecurity(securedEnabled = true, jsr250Enabled = true)
// On a @Configuration class. Then, on a service method:
@Secured("ROLE_ADMIN")
// OR (with jakarta.annotation.security.RolesAllowed):
@RolesAllowed("ADMIN")
// These are alternatives, not two annotations to stack here.

Use org.springframework.security.access.annotation.Secured for @Secured and jakarta.annotation.security.RolesAllowed for @RolesAllowed (on Spring Security 6 / Jakarta-based applications). Method security can complement HTTP authorization, not automatically replace it: an unprotected service operation is still reachable through any caller that can invoke it.

✓

Keep these ideas

01Opt in with @EnableMethodSecurity; an intercepted Spring-bean call enforces the rule.
02@PreAuthorize can inspect authorities and arguments before execution.
03@PostAuthorize can inspect returnObject, but cannot undo side effects.
04PermissionEvaluator moves richer object- or ID-based policies out of SpEL strings.

Check your understanding

Can a failed @PostAuthorize prevent a method from writing to a database?

No. The method has already executed. Depending on transaction and interceptor ordering, its transaction may already have committed. Use preauthorization for rules meant to prevent the operation itself.

Why might @PreAuthorize not run on an internal call within the same service instance?

Proxy-based Spring AOP intercepts calls that go through the proxy. Calling another method with this.method() inside the same bean normally bypasses it.

What differs between the two hasPermission overloads?

One receives an object, often after retrieval; the other receives its ID and type, allowing a pre-check that performs any necessary lookup itself.

Chapter 12 · Method-level filtering

Keep only
what fits.

Authorization does not always have to reject an entire call. Filtering can remove disallowed elements before a method receives a collection—or before its caller sees a returned collection.

PreFilter & PostFilterMutable collections10 book figures
The collection boundary
Nikolai + Julien itemsINPUT
owner == current userRULE
Only Nikolai itemsOUTPUT

Drop elements deliberately; reject the call when partial work is unsafe.

Chapter twelve

The big picture01 / Filter vs. deny02 / Before the call03 / Mutable input04 / After the call05 / Filter in the queryQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 12, “Implementing filtering at the method level” (book pp. 235–254). Figures 12.1–12.10 are embedded from the supplied PDF. The safe GET-only learning demo does not copy the book’s state-changing GET endpoint.
The 60-second takeaway

Filter the elements, not the entire call.

@PreFilter examines a collection argument before a method runs; @PostFilter examines a returned collection afterward. Their expression evaluates each filterObject against the authenticated user. Unlike @PreAuthorize and @PostAuthorize, an element that fails the filter is removed rather than causing the whole call to be denied. At database scale, apply ownership in the query before loading rows.

01

Filtering is not all-or-nothing

Chapter 11’s authorization annotations answer “may this method run?” or “may this result be exposed?” Filtering instead asks “which elements may flow through?” The method still runs, possibly with an empty list; the caller may still receive an empty list. The chapter focuses on arrays and collections; this guide’s examples use mutable Java lists.

Reject the operation

@PreAuthorize

No work is performed when the predicate fails. Prefer this for operations that must be all-or-nothing.

Keep eligible elements

@PreFilter

Spring processes only the elements matching the filter expression; a partial batch is expected behavior.

Partial success is a product decision. For payments, bulk deletes, or other sensitive mutations, silently discarding some requested items may mislead the user. Validate and reject the whole batch when that is your contract; do not substitute a filter for authorization of each persisted object.
02

Before the method receives a list

@PreFilter("filterObject.owner == authentication.name") evaluates each element in the selected collection argument. filterObject is the current product, while authentication.name comes from the authenticated security context. The interceptor removes nonmatching values before invoking the service.

The following read-only demo makes filtering visible without performing sales. Add its Java file to a Spring Boot app with web and security starters (and a matching package declaration). Remove competing demos from previous chapters. Set DEMO_PASSWORD locally. The list is created on the server to illustrate the mechanism; in a real write path, do not trust a client-supplied owner field to establish ownership—check persisted ownership by a trusted ID.

ProductFiltersDemo.java · runnable read-only learning app
import java.util.ArrayList;
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.method.configuration.EnableMethodSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreFilter;
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PostFilter;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
public class ProductFiltersDemo {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder encoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    String password = System.getenv("DEMO_PASSWORD");
    if (password == null || password.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set DEMO_PASSWORD for local testing");
    }
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(
        User.withUsername("nikolai").password(encoder.encode(password))
            .authorities("read").build(),
        User.withUsername("julien").password(encoder.encode(password))
            .authorities("read").build());
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain chain(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .build(); // CSRF stays enabled; both endpoints use safe GET
  }
}

class Product {
  private final String name;
  private final String owner;
  Product(String name, String owner) {
    this.name = name;
    this.owner = owner;
  }
  public String getName() { return name; }
  public String getOwner() { return owner; }
}

@Service
class ProductFilterService {
  private final List<Product> catalog = List.of(
      new Product("beer", "nikolai"),
      new Product("candy", "nikolai"),
      new Product("chocolate", "julien"));

  @PreFilter("filterObject.owner == authentication.name")
  public List<Product> previewOwned(List<Product> products) {
    return products; // An already-filtered, mutable list
  }

  @PostFilter("filterObject.owner == authentication.name")
  public List<Product> visibleProducts() {
    return new ArrayList<>(catalog); // New mutable result
  }

  public List<Product> catalogCopy() {
    return new ArrayList<>(catalog);
  }
}

@RestController
class ProductFilterController {
  private final ProductFilterService products;
  ProductFilterController(ProductFilterService products) { this.products = products; }

  @GetMapping("/products/preview")
  List<Product> preview() {
    return products.previewOwned(products.catalogCopy());
  }

  @GetMapping("/products/visible")
  List<Product> visible() { return products.visibleProducts(); }
}
Terminal · inspect both filters
# Nikolai sees beer and candy in either endpoint.
curl -i -u "nikolai:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/products/preview
curl -i -u "nikolai:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/products/visible

# Julien sees only chocolate in either endpoint.
curl -i -u "julien:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/products/preview
curl -i -u "julien:$DEMO_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/products/visible
03

The collection may be changed in place

In the book’s list example, prefiltering removes nonmatching items from the same list instance passed to the service. Passing List.of(...) instead causes UnsupportedOperationException when the interceptor tries to remove an element. The demo passes new ArrayList<>(...), and its postfilter result is mutable too.

Practical cautionIf the caller retains a reference to the mutable list, it may observe the changed contents after the call. Make an intentional copy at the boundary. Filtering support and mutation semantics differ among collection, array, map, and stream types and Spring Security versions; verify your specific type instead of assuming every container behaves like ArrayList.
04

After the method returns a list

@PostFilter lets the service fetch or produce a collection, then removes elements the caller must not receive. As with @PreFilter, filterObject stands for one element, and authentication.name identifies the current user. A nonmatching element is removed rather than denying the entire method call.

A filtered return is not cheap by default. The method has already fetched or created the entire collection. Postfiltering can prevent disclosure to its caller but does not reduce database reads, network cost, or in-memory processing that already happened.
05

At scale, filter in the data source

Annotating a Spring Data repository method that loads all products with @PostFilter still loads everyone’s rows first. This wastes memory and can become dangerous at scale. The chapter then adds the owner predicate to a query, so the database returns only rows for the authenticated user.

A straightforward modern alternative to the book’s security-context SpEL query is a derived repository method with an explicit owner parameter. Supply that parameter from the authenticated security context in a service, not from the client’s request. This snippet needs a Spring Data JPA entity named ProductEntity, its repository, a configured datasource, and appropriate database indexes; it is not part of the in-memory demo.

Spring Data recipe · fetch only owned matches
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.data.jpa.repository.JpaRepository;
import org.springframework.security.access.AccessDeniedException;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.AnonymousAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

interface ProductRepository extends JpaRepository<ProductEntity, Long> {
  List<ProductEntity> findByOwnerAndNameContainingIgnoreCase(
      String owner, String name);
}

@Service
class OwnedProductSearch {
  private final ProductRepository repository;
  OwnedProductSearch(ProductRepository repository) {
    this.repository = repository;
  }

  List<ProductEntity> search(String text) {
    Authentication user = SecurityContextHolder.getContext().getAuthentication();
    if (user == null || !user.isAuthenticated()
        || user instanceof AnonymousAuthenticationToken) {
      throw new AccessDeniedException("Authentication required");
    }
    return repository.findByOwnerAndNameContainingIgnoreCase(
        user.getName(), text);
  }
}

The book’s alternative registers a SecurityEvaluationContextExtension bean and uses Spring Data SpEL inside an @Query, such as p.owner = ?#{authentication.name}. Both approaches put ownership in the database query. The explicit parameter above is easier to review and test independently; whichever you use, scope counts and pagination by owner too. An untrusted username request parameter must never replace the authenticated principal in the ownership predicate.

Design checkLoading only owned records is both a security boundary and a performance choice. Review indexing, pagination, and any other query route that accesses the same data. When reading a single record, also enforce ownership on that lookup, rather than fetching all rows and filtering in Java.
✓

Keep these ideas

01@PreFilter removes disallowed argument elements before a method runs.
02@PostFilter removes disallowed result elements after a method runs.
03Use mutable lists for the book’s examples; immutable List.of(...) can fail when filtered.
04For repository reads, query only the current user’s records instead of loading everyone’s and postfiltering.

Check your understanding

What happens when every input element fails a prefilter?

Typically the method is still called with an empty collection. If your operation must reject an entirely unauthorized batch, use a separate validation or preauthorization rule.

Why can List.of(...) throw in the prefilter example?

The list is immutable. Spring Security’s list filtering in this example removes elements from the supplied list; use a mutable copy such as new ArrayList<>(source).

Does a postfilter make a findAll() database query safe and efficient?

No. It happens after the repository has loaded the rows. Put the ownership predicate in the query, and scope pagination and counts as well.

Chapter 13 · OAuth 2 & OpenID Connect

A token, not
a password.

Move from one application holding everyone’s credentials to separate roles: a client requests limited access, an authorization server issues a token, and a resource server decides whether to honor it.

OAuth actors & tokensGrants & PKCE13 book figures
The access path
Authorization serverISSUE
Client holds tokenPRESENT
Resource serverVERIFY

An access token is a limited, short-lived credential.

Chapter thirteen

The big picture01 / Four actors02 / Token shapes03 / Authorization code04 / Add PKCE05 / Other token paths06 / OpenID Connect07 / Security pitfallsQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 13, “What are OAuth 2 and OpenID Connect?” (book pp. 257–274). All thirteen numbered figures are embedded from the supplied PDF. Several simplified book diagrams are clarified in nearby text.
The 60-second takeaway

Separate authorization from the application holding the data.

OAuth 2 is a framework for delegated access: a client obtains an access token from an authorization server and presents it to a resource server. The resource server validates the token and enforces scopes and its own rules. OpenID Connect (OIDC) adds a standardized layer for user authentication, including an ID token. A token’s format, how it is obtained, and what it may access are different questions.

01

Four actors, separate responsibilities

The chapter compares an access token to a visitor card: the front desk checks an identity and issues a card limited to certain doors. In software, the user interacts with a client; the client obtains an access token; the resource server verifies it before allowing a requested operation.

Resource owner / userThe person whose resources or permissions are involved; some flows have no human present.
ClientThe application requesting access on a user’s behalf—or on its own behalf in machine-to-machine use.
Authorization serverAuthenticates as required, obtains authorization, and issues tokens with limited permissions.
Resource serverThe API receiving the access token; it verifies the token and makes a final access decision.
Distinguish the terms. OAuth 2 defines access delegation, not a general-purpose proof of a person’s identity to the client. Use OIDC when the client needs standardized user sign-in. An access token authorizes API calls; it is not an ID token.
02

Tokens can be opaque or self-contained

An access token is a credential presented by the client, typically as Authorization: Bearer <access-token>. It may be an opaque reference the API must introspect, or a signed self-contained token such as a JWT. Format does not decide the OAuth grant type.

Opaque reference

Ask the issuer

Introspection can provide current token status and metadata; it introduces a dependency on the issuer or an appropriately managed cache.

Signed JWT

Verify locally

The API checks the signature using trusted keys plus issuer, expiry, audience, and permissions. Keys and token lifetime require operational care.

Do not confuse encoded with encryptedJWT header and payload are normally readable by anyone holding the token. A valid signature proves integrity and trusted issuance, not confidentiality or that the token is meant for this particular API. Check issuer, audience, expiry, signature/key policy, and the requested scope or authority. Do not put secrets in an ordinary signed JWT.
03

Authorization code: redirect, then exchange

For interactive user access, the client sends the browser to the authorization server. After login and any required consent, the authorization server redirects back with a short-lived authorization code. The client exchanges that code at the token endpoint for an access token. The code is not itself the token used at the API.

01 / StartClient generates a fresh state and PKCE pair, then sends the browser to the authorization endpoint with the registered redirect URI.
02 / ReturnAuthorization server redirects to that URI with a code and state; the client verifies the returned state.
03 / ExchangeClient exchanges the code and PKCE verifier for an access token. A confidential client also authenticates itself as appropriate.
Book-diagram clarification. The figure says a stolen code cannot be used without a client secret. That applies to confidential clients able to protect one. Browser and native applications are public clients; embedding a secret in them does not make it secret. Use authorization code with PKCE, validated state, registered exact redirect URIs, and HTTPS. PKCE and client authentication solve different problems.
04

PKCE binds the code to its requester

Proof Key for Code Exchange adds a one-time, high-entropy code_verifier known to the initiating client. Send its S256 code_challenge in the authorization request, then send the original verifier at the token endpoint. The server recomputes and compares before issuing a token. Intercepting the authorization code alone is not enough.

For S256, generate at least 32 unpredictable random bytes, encode the verifier with unpadded Base64url, hash its ASCII bytes with SHA-256, and encode the hash the same way for the challenge. This Java 17+ record illustrates the transformation; keep the verifier private to the initiating client and never log or place it in the initial redirect.

PkcePair.java · generate an S256 verifier and challenge
import java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets;
import java.security.MessageDigest;
import java.security.NoSuchAlgorithmException;
import java.security.SecureRandom;
import java.util.Base64;

public record PkcePair(String verifier, String challenge) {
  public static PkcePair create() throws NoSuchAlgorithmException {
    byte[] random = new byte[32];
    new SecureRandom().nextBytes(random);
    String verifier = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding()
        .encodeToString(random);
    byte[] digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
        .digest(verifier.getBytes(StandardCharsets.US_ASCII));
    String challenge = Base64.getUrlEncoder().withoutPadding()
        .encodeToString(digest);
    return new PkcePair(verifier, challenge);
  }
}

Use your framework’s OAuth client support for the complete flow rather than hand-building authorization requests in production. The generated pair is per authorization attempt; store it only for the duration of the flow. PKCE is not a substitute for validating state or for protecting access and refresh tokens after issuance.

05

No user? Or an expired access token?

Client credentials lets a confidential service authenticate and obtain a token for its own access, without a user’s login. A refresh token, when issued, lets an authorized client request a new short-lived access token without making the person sign in again. They solve different situations: a grant type versus a way to renew a prior authorization.

Client credentials

App acts as itself

Use only when a client can protect its credential. An end-user authorization is not implied by the resulting token.

Refresh token

Longer-lived power

Not every client receives one. Store it carefully, rotate it where supported, and revoke it when compromised or no longer needed.

Deprecated patternsDo not choose the implicit or resource-owner password-credentials grants for new applications. Prefer authorization code with PKCE for interactive sign-in and client credentials for an authorized confidential service. Access tokens should be short-lived; refresh tokens require a separate lifecycle and strict storage.
06

OIDC adds an identity layer

OAuth access tokens are for resource servers. OpenID Connect builds an authentication protocol on OAuth 2: requesting the openid scope can yield an ID token about the authenticated user for the client. Optional scopes such as profile can make additional claims available. The authorization server is often called an identity provider (IdP).

Access tokenPresented to an API to authorize a resource request; the API validates that token for its own audience.
ID tokenConsumed by the client to establish sign-in; validate issuer, signature, audience (client ID), expiry, and nonce where applicable.
ScopeDescribes requested delegated access or OIDC data; receiving a scope does not override an API’s own authorization policy.
DiscoveryOIDC providers commonly publish standardized metadata and signing keys, enabling interoperable clients.
Never swap the tokens. A resource server must not accept an ID token in place of an access token: its intended audience is the client. Likewise, an OAuth access token by itself is not a standardized proof of who signed in to your client.

For a Spring Security resource server, a conceptual JWT configuration looks like the fragment below. It is not a complete runnable OAuth deployment: add the OAuth2 resource-server dependency, put this class in your application package, set the issuer URI to your real provider, configure audience validation for your API, and test valid and invalid tokens. The example grants only a read scope to one API path; it keeps CSRF behavior unchanged.

Resource-server recipe · requires a real issuer and audience policy
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
class ApiSecurity {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers("/health").permitAll()
        .requestMatchers("/invoices/**")
            .hasAuthority("SCOPE_invoices.read")
        .anyRequest().denyAll())
      .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
      .build();
  }
}
application.properties · illustrative issuer address
# Replace with your provider's actual issuer URL.
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=https://id.example.com/issuer
# Also configure a validator for your API audience.

For this kind of Spring Security configuration, JWT scopes are commonly mapped to authorities with a SCOPE_ prefix. If the issuer uses different claim shapes, configure an appropriate converter instead of assuming every token has the required authority. An opaque-token resource server uses token introspection rather than JWT verification.

07

Treat bearer tokens as valuable secrets

The chapter closes with common failure modes: CSRF around a logged-in client, exposed client credentials, stolen or replayed access tokens, and hijacked refresh tokens. A bearer token can be used by whoever has it until it expires or is revoked or rejected. The protocol does not compensate for unsafe storage, broad scopes, or missing API checks.

Secure the redirectValidate state on callback, use exact registered redirect URIs, HTTPS, and PKCE. For OIDC, validate the ID token and nonce where required.
Constrain the tokenCheck signature or introspection status, issuer, audience, expiry, and scopes. Do not send bearer tokens in URLs or diagnostic logs.
Protect renewalKeep client secrets and refresh tokens out of exposed browser code; apply rotation and revocation policies where available.
Related chaptersChapter 9’s CSRF protections still matter for cookie-authenticated OAuth clients; chapter 10’s CORS policy still governs browser cross-origin responses. Neither one replaces OAuth token validation. Chapter 14 moves from these concepts to implementing an authorization server.
✓

Keep these ideas

01OAuth 2 delegates access: client → authorization server → access token → resource server.
02Opaque tokens need introspection; signed JWTs can be validated locally but their payload is readable.
03Use authorization code + PKCE for interactive clients, client credentials for confidential machine clients.
04OIDC adds user sign-in and an ID token for the client; an API should expect an access token.

Check your understanding

Is an authorization code the credential a client sends to the resource server?

No. The code is exchanged at the authorization server’s token endpoint. The resulting access token is what the client presents to the API.

Does a valid JWT signature prove an API should accept the token?

No. The API must also check issuer, audience, expiry, and relevant scopes or permissions. A signed token intended for a different API is not sufficient.

Can a public browser client safely rely on a client secret instead of PKCE?

No. A secret embedded in browser-delivered code is not confidential. PKCE binds the authorization code to the initiating client’s one-time verifier.

Chapter 14 · OAuth 2 authorization server

Issue with
intent.

An authorization server authenticates users and clients, registers what each client may request, and issues access tokens. This chapter assembles the moving pieces and follows code, client-credentials, opaque-token, and revocation flows.

Chapter fourteen

The big picture01 / The components02 / Wire the server03 / Code + PKCE04 / Client credentials05 / Opaque tokens06 / RevocationQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 14, “Implementing an OAuth 2 authorization server” (book pp. 275–296). All eight numbered figures are embedded. The book-era Spring Authorization Server API and temporary in-memory stores are identified as learning choices, not production defaults.
The 60-second takeaway

The issuer is its own security-critical application.

Spring Authorization Server supplies OAuth 2/OIDC protocol endpoints. You provide user authentication, registered clients, signing keys, and server settings. A client may use authorization code with PKCE or client credentials; its access tokens may be signed JWTs or opaque references. Discovery advertises endpoints; introspection and revocation manage token status. Production needs stable keys, persistent state, HTTPS, and carefully registered redirect URIs.

01

The moving parts

The authorization server is not the API. It handles authentication and token issuance; a resource server receives access tokens and decides whether an API request is authorized. The book begins by splitting server concerns into protocol endpoints, login/security, user details, client registrations, key material, and general settings.

Protocol filter chainHandles authorization, token, JWK, introspection, revocation, and optional OIDC endpoints; higher priority than the general chain.
Login filter chainHandles user login and other app requests; do not accidentally route protocol requests through it.
UserDetailsServiceDescribes human users for interactive flows, with password hashes and authorities.
RegisteredClientRepositoryStores client IDs, hashed secrets or public-client policy, grants, redirect URIs, and allowed scopes.
JWKSourceSupplies signing keys for JWTs and public key material for verification.
AuthorizationServerSettingsConfigures issuer identity and endpoint paths. Set the public issuer explicitly in real deployments.
02

Wire a small learning issuer

The following Spring Boot 3 / Spring Authorization Server 1.x-era learning skeleton follows the book’s two-chain setup. It uses the spring-boot-starter-oauth2-authorization-server and web starters, in-memory users and clients, BCrypt-hashed secrets, a temporary RSA signing key, and OIDC. Put it in your Boot application package with a matching package declaration. It is not a deployable identity provider.

AuthorizationServerStudyConfig.java · two chains and client registrations
import java.security.KeyPair;
import java.security.KeyPairGenerator;
import java.security.NoSuchAlgorithmException;
import java.security.interfaces.RSAPrivateKey;
import java.security.interfaces.RSAPublicKey;
import java.time.Duration;
import java.util.UUID;
import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.JWKSet;
import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.RSAKey;
import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.source.ImmutableJWKSet;
import com.nimbusds.jose.jwk.source.JWKSource;
import com.nimbusds.jose.proc.SecurityContext;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.core.annotation.Order;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.AuthorizationGrantType;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.ClientAuthenticationMethod;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.core.oidc.OidcScopes;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.JwtDecoder;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.client.RegisteredClient;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.client.RegisteredClientRepository;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.client.InMemoryRegisteredClientRepository;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.config.annotation.web.configuration.OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfiguration;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.config.annotation.web.configurers.OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfigurer;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.settings.AuthorizationServerSettings;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.settings.ClientSettings;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.settings.TokenSettings;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.security.web.authentication.LoginUrlAuthenticationEntryPoint;

@Configuration
public class AuthorizationServerStudyConfig {
  @Bean @Order(1)
  SecurityFilterChain protocols(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfiguration.applyDefaultSecurity(http);
    http.getConfigurer(OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfigurer.class)
        .oidc(Customizer.withDefaults());
    http.exceptionHandling(e -> e.authenticationEntryPoint(
        new LoginUrlAuthenticationEntryPoint("/login")));
    return http.build();
  }

  @Bean @Order(2)
  SecurityFilterChain login(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
        .formLogin(Customizer.withDefaults()).build();
  }

  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder encoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  private static String required(String key) {
    String value = System.getenv(key);
    if (value == null || value.isBlank()) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Set " + key + " for the local exercise");
    }
    return value;
  }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(User.withUsername("bill")
        .password(encoder.encode(required("DEMO_USER_PASSWORD")))
        .roles("USER").build());
  }

  @Bean
  RegisteredClientRepository clients(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    RegisteredClient browser = RegisteredClient.withId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
        .clientId("web-client")
        .clientSecret(encoder.encode(required("DEMO_WEB_CLIENT_SECRET")))
        .clientAuthenticationMethod(ClientAuthenticationMethod.CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC)
        .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.AUTHORIZATION_CODE)
        .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.REFRESH_TOKEN)
        .redirectUri("https://app.example.com/callback")
        .scope(OidcScopes.OPENID)
        .clientSettings(ClientSettings.builder().requireProofKey(true).build())
        .build();
    RegisteredClient service = RegisteredClient.withId(UUID.randomUUID().toString())
        .clientId("service-client")
        .clientSecret(encoder.encode(required("DEMO_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET")))
        .clientAuthenticationMethod(ClientAuthenticationMethod.CLIENT_SECRET_BASIC)
        .authorizationGrantType(AuthorizationGrantType.CLIENT_CREDENTIALS)
        .scope("invoices.read")
        .tokenSettings(TokenSettings.builder()
            .accessTokenTimeToLive(Duration.ofMinutes(5)).build())
        .build();
    return new InMemoryRegisteredClientRepository(browser, service);
  }

  @Bean
  JWKSource<SecurityContext> jwkSource() throws NoSuchAlgorithmException {
    KeyPairGenerator generator = KeyPairGenerator.getInstance("RSA");
    generator.initialize(2048);
    KeyPair pair = generator.generateKeyPair();
    RSAKey key = new RSAKey.Builder((RSAPublicKey) pair.getPublic())
        .privateKey((RSAPrivateKey) pair.getPrivate())
        .keyID(UUID.randomUUID().toString()).build();
    return new ImmutableJWKSet<>(new JWKSet(key));
  }

  @Bean
  JwtDecoder jwtDecoder(JWKSource<SecurityContext> source) {
    return OAuth2AuthorizationServerConfiguration.jwtDecoder(source);
  }

  @Bean
  AuthorizationServerSettings settings() {
    return AuthorizationServerSettings.builder().build();
  }
}
Learning setup onlyThe code generates a signing key on each restart and keeps registrations and issued authorizations in memory. Restarting invalidates prior JWT signatures and loses server-side state. For a real issuer, use persistent client/authorization/consent stores, stable protected keys with rotation and a published JWKS, distinct strong secrets, an explicit public issuer behind your proxy, HTTPS, monitoring, and an actual registered callback. Do not use the book’s plaintext client secret or NoOp password encoder. The applyDefaultSecurity API follows the book’s Spring Authorization Server 1.x generation; check your library version for newer DSL alternatives.
03

Discover endpoints, then exchange a code

With OIDC enabled, discovery at /.well-known/openid-configuration advertises the public issuer and endpoints. The book uses /oauth2/authorize for the browser redirect, /oauth2/token for token exchange, and /oauth2/jwks for public signing keys. Clients must use the configured issuer and exact redirect URI, not guess endpoint paths.

The web-client study registration above is a confidential web client: it has a BCrypt-protected client secret and requires PKCE. The public-looking app.example.com URI is illustrative, not a working local callback. To complete the flow, build a genuine callback, register its exact URI, generate a fresh state and S256 challenge per request, verify state on return, then redeem the code once with the matching verifier and client authentication. Do not disable PKCE just to simplify the demo.

GET /oauth2/authorizeBrowser redirects with response_type=code, client ID, exact redirect URI, scope, state, and PKCE challenge.
POST /oauth2/tokenClient submits the code, redirect URI, and verifier. A confidential client also authenticates, here with HTTP Basic using its client ID and secret.
Token responseContains an access token and metadata; with openid, an ID token may also be returned. The resource API expects the access token, not the ID token.
Terminal · inspect discovery and public keys locally
# These are terminal requests to YOUR locally running study server.
curl -i http://localhost:8080/.well-known/openid-configuration
curl -i http://localhost:8080/oauth2/jwks

# Inspect the exact authorization_endpoint, token_endpoint,
# jwks_uri, introspection_endpoint, and revocation_endpoint
# in your server's discovery response.
Redirect caveat. Figure 14.6 intentionally shows a 404 at the book’s nonexistent callback URL; that is not a working OAuth client. Never harvest an authorization code from an arbitrary page or paste secrets into a real third-party redirect. Use a callback you control over HTTPS, registered precisely for your client.
04

Let a service act as itself

The client credentials grant has no end-user sign-in. A confidential service authenticates at the token endpoint and asks for the scopes allowed by its RegisteredClient. The example’s service-client is registered for client_credentials and invoices.read, not for an OIDC user identity.

Terminal · request a short-lived service token
# Set DEMO_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET in your terminal environment.
# curl -u handles the Basic header; do not paste a Base64 secret.
curl -i -u "service-client:$DEMO_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -X POST http://localhost:8080/oauth2/token \
  -d 'grant_type=client_credentials' \
  -d 'scope=invoices.read'

# The response contains an access_token, token_type=Bearer,
# and a short expires_in. Do not paste real tokens into logs.

This command is for a locally started learning server in a terminal. The result is not proof that any particular API should accept the token; the resource server (chapter 15) must validate it for its own audience and authorization requirements. Avoid treating an issued scope as carte blanche.

05

Switch token format, then introspect

The book changes a registered client’s TokenSettings to OAuth2TokenFormat.REFERENCE to issue opaque access tokens instead of signed JWTs. The token endpoint flow is otherwise similar. A resource server with an opaque token asks the issuer’s /oauth2/introspect endpoint whether it is active and what scope or subject it represents.

Opaque format · alternative client registration fragment
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.settings.OAuth2TokenFormat;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.authorization.settings.TokenSettings;

// In a RegisteredClient builder, replace the tokenSettings
// used for that client (do not paste this as a second bean):
.tokenSettings(TokenSettings.builder()
    .accessTokenFormat(OAuth2TokenFormat.REFERENCE)
    .accessTokenTimeToLive(Duration.ofMinutes(5))
    .build())

Introspection is a server-to-server call. The resource server needs its own authorized credentials to introspect; the response contains active: true for a live token, and active: false for a missing, expired, or revoked one. Use a form-encoded POST and TLS rather than putting bearer tokens in query strings; caching decisions affect how quickly revocation becomes visible.

Storage requirementAn opaque reference has no self-contained claims to verify offline. The authorization server must keep a durable token/authorization record, and the resource server must be able to contact the introspection service (or use a carefully bounded cache). In-memory storage from the study skeleton disappears on restart.
06

Revocation is a status change

The issuer exposes /oauth2/revoke to invalidate a previously issued token. After a successful revocation, introspection should report it inactive. But a resource server that only checks a JWT signature and expiry offline may continue accepting that JWT until it expires: it has not learned the server-side status change.

Opaque token

Ask each time

Introspection can reflect revocation promptly, subject to caching and service availability.

Signed JWT

Offline until expiry

Signature-only validation cannot see revocation. Use short lifetimes, introspection, a denylist, or another deliberate strategy if prompt invalidation matters.

Terminal · inspect and revoke a test token
# A configured introspection client needs its own credentials.
# The study client is used here only for an isolated local test.
curl -u "service-client:$DEMO_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -X POST http://localhost:8080/oauth2/introspect \
  --data-urlencode "token=$TEST_ACCESS_TOKEN"

curl -u "service-client:$DEMO_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET" \
  -X POST http://localhost:8080/oauth2/revoke \
  --data-urlencode "token=$TEST_ACCESS_TOKEN"

# Introspect again; expect active=false for a revoked token.
# Never put the token in a query string or paste real values in chat.
Know what you are invalidating. A token revocation endpoint can acknowledge a request without revealing whether the submitted value existed. Test with an actual token owned by the authorized client and an authenticated introspection caller. Keep short access-token lifetimes; do not copy the book’s deliberately long 12-hour teaching expiry into a live system.
✓

Keep these ideas

01Two ordered chains separate OAuth/OIDC protocol endpoints from the normal login flow.
02RegisteredClientRepository manages applications; UserDetailsService manages people.
03Authorization code + PKCE involves a real callback and verifier; client credentials has no user login.
04JWT signing requires stable keys; opaque tokens depend on token records and introspection. Revocation visibility depends on validation strategy.

Check your understanding

Why should a production authorization server not generate a new RSA key on every restart?

Previously issued JWTs signed by the old private key could no longer be validated once its public key disappears. Store keys safely and rotate them in a planned way.

Does client_credentials authenticate a user?

No. It authenticates a client acting on its own behalf. The resulting token must not be treated as evidence of a human’s login.

Does revoking a JWT automatically stop an API that verifies only signature and expiry?

No. That API does not consult the issuer for live status. Use an appropriate online check or another revocation strategy when immediate invalidation is required.
