Chapter 15 · OAuth 2 resource server

Verify before
you serve.

The authorization server issues access tokens; the resource server protects the API. Validate the token’s origin, lifetime, intended audience, and permissions before returning data or performing an action.

JWT & JWKSIntrospection10 book figures
The API boundary
Bearer access tokenREQUEST
Signature or introspectionVERIFY
Audience + scope + policyDECIDE

A well-formed token is not automatically an authorized request.

Chapter fifteen

The big picture01 / Protect the API02 / Verify JWTs03 / Custom claims04 / Introspection05 / Multiple issuersQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 15, “Implementing an OAuth 2 resource server” (book pp. 297–323). All ten numbered figures are embedded from the supplied PDF. The book’s permissive claim converter and client-selected authentication route are discussed with safer alternatives.
The 60-second takeaway

The API is the enforcement point.

A resource server receives Authorization: Bearer <access-token>. For signed JWTs it verifies a signature with trusted public keys; for opaque tokens it calls an authenticated introspection endpoint. Both need an authorization policy, not just token parsing. Custom claims can inform a decision after validation. If multiple issuers exist, trust only configured issuers and bind each request to the correct tenant.

01

A resource server is your backend

The client requests a token from an authorization server, then presents it to a separate backend. That backend is the resource server: it safeguards data and operations. It may work with an authorization server you build yourself (chapter 14) or one operated by another provider.

Authentication

Is this token valid?

Verify signature and trusted issuer or introspection activity, time bounds, token type, and the intended audience. A missing or invalid token normally results in 401.

Authorization

May it do this?

Check scopes and resource-specific rules after token validation. A valid token with insufficient permission normally results in 403.

Bearer means possession. Anyone who obtains a valid bearer access token can attempt to use it until expiry or rejection. Never accept a token merely because it parses, and never use an OIDC ID token as an API access token.
02

Verify signed JWTs with trusted keys

The issuer signs access tokens with a private key and publishes the matching public keys as a JWKS. The API obtains the JWKS URI from trusted issuer metadata and checks the JWT signature. Signature verification is only part of validation: also require the expected issuer, valid time window, the intended API audience, and sufficient scope.

This modernized study recipe uses Spring Boot’s web, security, and spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server starters. Put the Java class in your application package with a matching package declaration, and run against a real trusted JWT issuer. The sample protects a single GET endpoint with the scope registered for the service client in chapter 14. Its issuer property is local-only; do not use it behind a public proxy without setting the actual issuer and audience.

InvoiceResourceSecurity.java · JWT-based API rule
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.annotation.AuthenticationPrincipal;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.Jwt;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@Configuration
public class InvoiceResourceSecurity {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/invoices")
            .hasAuthority("SCOPE_invoices.read")
        .anyRequest().denyAll())
      .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
      .build();
  }
}

@RestController
class InvoiceResourceController {
  @GetMapping("/invoices")
  String invoices(@AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt jwt) {
    return "Invoices for " + jwt.getSubject();
  }
}
application.properties · learning issuer and API port
# When the chapter 14 issuer runs on this same machine:
server.port=9090
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=http://localhost:8080
# Production: use its exact HTTPS public issuer. Once the issuer
# adds invoices-api to access-token audiences, require it here:
# spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences=invoices-api

An issuer-uri configuration derives trusted JWKS metadata and validates the issuer and token time claims. A bare jwk-set-uri is not enough to check who issued the token unless issuer validation is configured separately. An actual API must also validate its audience; the chapter 14 study client may not issue an audience value for this sample API by default. Configure the issuer to add an API audience and then enable the commented Spring Boot audience property above; do not deploy the sample without this check. Do not interpret openid as a substitute for an API read scope.

Terminal · call the API with a test access token
# Set ACCESS_TOKEN to a real access token issued for this API.
# Do not use an id_token, or put tokens in URLs or logs.
curl -i -H "Authorization: Bearer $ACCESS_TOKEN" \
  http://localhost:9090/invoices

# Missing token: 401. Valid token without invoices.read: 403.
curl -i http://localhost:9090/invoices
03

Claims become an authenticated principal

The book adds a priority claim to a JWT on the issuer and illustrates a converter that builds a custom JwtAuthenticationToken containing that value. After token validation, the converter can map claims and scopes into the Authentication stored in the security context. The service can then use the claim in its own authorization logic.

The book’s demonstration gives every converted token a dummy read authority. Do not copy that as an access policy. This alternative configuration retains Spring Security’s scope-to-SCOPE_ authority mapping while exposing priority for optional business checks. Use it instead of InvoiceResourceSecurity in the same app, with the same issuer property and controller; it does not replace issuer or audience validation.

PriorityInvoiceSecurity.java · alternative JWT configuration
import java.util.Collection;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.GrantedAuthority;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.jwt.Jwt;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.resource.authentication.JwtAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.resource.authentication.JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
class PriorityInvoiceSecurity {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter scopes = new JwtGrantedAuthoritiesConverter();
    return http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/invoices")
            .hasAuthority("SCOPE_invoices.read")
        .anyRequest().denyAll())
      .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(jwt ->
          jwt.jwtAuthenticationConverter(token ->
              new PriorityAuthentication(token, scopes.convert(token)))))
      .build();
  }
}

class PriorityAuthentication extends JwtAuthenticationToken {
  private final String priority;
  PriorityAuthentication(Jwt jwt, Collection<? extends GrantedAuthority> grants) {
    super(jwt, grants);
    this.priority = jwt.getClaimAsString("priority");
  }
  public String getPriority() { return priority; }
}
Claim hygieneOnly use claims from a token whose signature, issuer, audience, and expiry you have validated. Missing or unexpected priority should grant no extra access. Do not serialize and return the whole authentication object to ordinary API callers just to inspect it; the book does so for an isolated demonstration.
04

Opaque tokens need an issuer call

For an opaque reference, the API cannot locally verify JWT claims. Instead it sends the token to the authorization server’s introspection endpoint with its own registered client credentials. The response tells the API whether the token is active and provides scope and other metadata. The same online check can reveal a revoked JWT’s status if the issuer supports introspection for it.

The alternative configuration below is not an additional filter chain to paste beside the JWT demo. Use the same authorizeHttpRequests rule with oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.opaqueToken(...)), and register a dedicated introspection client at the issuer. Keep credentials out of source control. The property names shown use Spring Boot’s opaquetoken prefix.

Opaque-token mode · alternative to JWT validation
// Replace oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(...))
// in the JWT chain; keep your endpoint authorization rules:
.oauth2ResourceServer(oauth ->
    oauth.opaqueToken(Customizer.withDefaults()))

// In application.properties (separate file):
// spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.opaquetoken.introspection-uri=https://issuer.example.com/oauth2/introspect
// spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.opaquetoken.client-id=${INTROSPECTION_CLIENT_ID}
// spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.opaquetoken.client-secret=${INTROSPECTION_CLIENT_SECRET}

A JWT resource server with local signature checks does not automatically notice issuer-side revocation. Introspection can provide fresher status, but a cache delays detection. For any token type, verify that introspection corresponds to the expected issuer and intended API; do not infer authorization from active alone.

05

Several issuers require a trusted resolver

A multitenant API may accept tokens from more than one trusted authorization server. An AuthenticationManagerResolver selects the manager that validates a given request. For several JWT issuers, Spring Security offers JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver; for mixed JWT and opaque tokens, a custom resolver can compose different providers.

For JWT-only multitenancy, allowlist exact issuer identifiers from configuration. This separate fragment replaces the single-issuer JWT configuration rather than being added to it. Consult your Spring Security version for the available resolver factory signature.

TrustedIssuerSecurity.java · separate JWT multitenant recipe
import jakarta.servlet.http.HttpServletRequest;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.AuthenticationManagerResolver;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.server.resource.authentication.JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
class TrustedIssuerSecurity {
  @Bean
  AuthenticationManagerResolver<HttpServletRequest> trustedIssuers(
      @Value("${security.issuers.primary}") String primary,
      @Value("${security.issuers.secondary}") String secondary) {
    return JwtIssuerAuthenticationManagerResolver.fromTrustedIssuers(
        primary, secondary);
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain api(HttpSecurity http,
      AuthenticationManagerResolver<HttpServletRequest> trustedIssuers)
      throws Exception {
    return http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/invoices")
            .hasAuthority("SCOPE_invoices.read")
        .anyRequest().denyAll())
      .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth ->
          oauth.authenticationManagerResolver(trustedIssuers))
      .build();
  }
}

Set security.issuers.primary and security.issuers.secondary to exact, deployment-approved issuer URLs. The iss claim can be used to select from this fixed allowlist, but only a successful validation against the selected issuer authenticates it. Use this configuration instead of either single-issuer chain, and enforce audience for each issuer: the single-issuer Boot audience property is not a substitute for per-tenant validation in this custom resolver.

Book correctionThe book’s mixed-token example chooses between JWT and opaque validation using a caller-supplied type header. An attacker can change that header. If you genuinely need multiple strategies, bind tenant selection to a route/hostname established and enforced by your deployment (not an untrusted Host header) or a verified issuer and maintain explicit per-tenant audience/scope rules; do not take an unverified token claim or arbitrary request header as permission to choose a weaker validator. Prevent untrusted issuer URLs from causing metadata fetches (SSRF).
✓

Keep these ideas

01JWT verification requires trusted keys, issuer and time checks, an API audience, and an authorization rule.
02Never equate a decoded claim with a validated token; converters must preserve real permissions.
03Opaque tokens require authenticated introspection; revocation visibility depends on online checks and caching.
04Multitenant validation needs an issuer allowlist and trusted tenant routing, not a caller-chosen security mode.

Check your understanding

Why is configuring only a JWKS URL weaker than configuring a trusted issuer?

The JWKS supplies signature keys, but without an issuer check the API may not establish who issued the token. Validate issuer and audience as well as signature and lifetime.

Can an API use an OIDC ID token for /invoices?

No. ID tokens are intended for the client application, while the resource server expects an access token intended for the API.

Will a locally validated JWT immediately reflect issuer-side revocation?

No. Signature and expiry checks alone cannot see a server-side status change. Use appropriate introspection, denylisting, or short lifetimes for your revocation requirements.

Chapter 16 · Implementing an OAuth 2 client

The other side
of the call.

A web application can send a person to an identity provider to sign in. A backend service can become a client of another API. Spring Security handles both, but the grants and the identities behind them are different.

OAuth 2 loginClient credentials11 book figures
Two client roles
Person signs in via providerLOGIN
Service requests its own tokenMACHINE
API checks that tokenRESOURCE

An app can be a resource server and a client at once.

Chapter sixteen

The big picture01 / Login providers02 / Your own issuer03 / Registrations04 / The signed-in user05 / Service credentials06 / Call an APIQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 16, “Implementing an OAuth 2 client” (book pp. 324–343). All 11 numbered figures are embedded. The book’s public token-returning demo is explained, not reproduced as a safe endpoint.
The 60-second takeaway

A client is a role, not a UI.

With oauth2Login(), the client is a web app that redirects a browser through an authorization-code flow and then establishes an authenticated session. With client credentials, a backend requests an access token for itself and calls another service. Neither flow replaces the resource server’s token validation and authorization from chapter 15.

01

Sign people in with a provider

The app acts as an OAuth 2 client when it sends a browser to Google, GitHub, or another provider. Spring Security’s oauth2Login() handles the redirect, callback, code exchange, and local authenticated session. Google can also provide OpenID Connect identity; GitHub’s usual login integration is OAuth 2 with user information, not automatically OIDC.

For a Spring Boot MVC application, add spring-boot-starter-web, spring-boot-starter-security, and spring-boot-starter-oauth2-client. Register a real HTTPS callback for your app at each provider. For a local learning run, providers may allow a localhost callback. Keep client secrets in environment variables or a secret manager, not in a repository.

WebLoginSecurity.java · web login configuration
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
class WebLoginSecurity {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain web(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth ->
        auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
      .oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults())
      .build();
  }
}
application.properties · Google and optional GitHub
server.port=7070
server.servlet.session.cookie.name=CLIENT_SESSION
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.google.client-id=${GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID}
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.google.client-secret=${GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET}
# Add GitHub only after registering another callback and setting both variables:
# spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.github.client-id=${GITHUB_CLIENT_ID}
# spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.github.client-secret=${GITHUB_CLIENT_SECRET}

The default callback is {baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}—for this local Google example, http://localhost:7070/login/oauth2/code/google. With one provider, visiting a protected page (such as /me from section 04 below) starts login; with several, Spring Security’s default login page lets users choose. The browser returns with a session cookie; this is not an access token intended for an arbitrary API.

Login is not API authorization. Use OIDC when you need a standardized identity assertion and the provider supports it; do not treat an arbitrary OAuth access token as proof of a person’s identity. Keep state, redirect-URI checks, CSRF protection, HTTPS, and secure session cookies enabled. Review account linking before merging identities from different providers.
02

Use your own OIDC issuer

A well-behaved OpenID Connect issuer exposes discovery metadata, so a client configured with its exact issuer-uri can discover its authorization, token, and JWKS endpoints. In an OIDC login, the client validates the ID token using trusted issuer keys; a separate resource server validates access tokens meant for its API. A plain OAuth-only provider also needs appropriate user-info/principal mapping—not just a JWKS URL.

This is a separate alternative to the Google/GitHub properties above. To use the chapter 14 issuer on http://localhost:8080, update its web-client registration to allow the exact local redirect URI below, leave its openid scope enabled, and retain requireProofKey(true). Supply the same DEMO_WEB_CLIENT_SECRET to both processes. Do not reuse the issuer’s service-client registration: that client has a different grant and scope.

Chapter 14 issuer · local-only registered redirect fragment
// Change the web-client RegisteredClient builder in the chapter 14 issuer:
// Replace its HTTPS example callback for this local learning run only.
.redirectUri("http://localhost:7070/login/oauth2/code/my-issuer")
// Keep authorization_code, scope(openid), and requireProofKey(true).
// Use HTTPS and your real exact callback in a deployed environment.
application.properties · custom local OIDC provider
server.port=7070
server.servlet.session.cookie.name=CLIENT_SESSION
spring.security.oauth2.client.provider.my-issuer.issuer-uri=http://localhost:8080
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-issuer.provider=my-issuer
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-issuer.client-id=web-client
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-issuer.client-secret=${DEMO_WEB_CLIENT_SECRET}
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-issuer.client-authentication-method=client_secret_basic
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-issuer.authorization-grant-type=authorization_code
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-issuer.redirect-uri={baseUrl}/login/oauth2/code/{registrationId}
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-issuer.scope=openid
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.my-issuer.client-name=Local issuer

Use the same WebLoginSecurity chain as above, but the chapter 14 issuer requires PKCE even for its confidential web-client. Configure this resolver instead of the default oauth2Login(Customizer.withDefaults()) in that chain. It adds a challenge to the authorization request; Spring Security retains the verifier through the callback.

OIDC login chain · PKCE alternative for the local issuer
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.registration.ClientRegistrationRepository;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.web.DefaultOAuth2AuthorizationRequestResolver;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.web.OAuth2AuthorizationRequestCustomizers;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;

@Configuration
class LocalOidcLoginSecurity {
  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain web(HttpSecurity http,
      ClientRegistrationRepository registrations) throws Exception {
    var resolver = new DefaultOAuth2AuthorizationRequestResolver(
        registrations, "/oauth2/authorization");
    resolver.setAuthorizationRequestCustomizer(
        OAuth2AuthorizationRequestCustomizers.withPkce());
    return http.authorizeHttpRequests(auth ->
        auth.anyRequest().authenticated())
      .oauth2Login(oauth -> oauth.authorizationEndpoint(endpoint ->
          endpoint.authorizationRequestResolver(resolver)))
      .build();
  }
}
Local-host detailBrowsers do not isolate cookies by port. Giving the client a distinct session cookie name avoids clashing with the chapter 14 issuer’s default session cookie when both use localhost. In production use HTTPS issuer/callback addresses, review reverse-proxy forwarded headers, and set secure cookie attributes; never blindly trust forwarded-host values.
03

Registrations are replaceable configuration

ClientRegistration stores a client’s grant, credentials, redirect and provider details. ClientRegistrationRepository looks registrations up by their IDs. Boot builds these objects from spring.security.oauth2.client.* properties, but a custom repository can load them from a protected store instead.

One registration

How this client talks

Its ID identifies the provider in login URLs and callbacks; credentials and allowed grant must match what the issuer registered.

A repository

Where registrations live

In-memory is easy to study; a vault or database implementation must handle availability, rotation, and consistent lookups.

GoogleRegistration.java · alternative repository bean
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.security.config.oauth2.client.CommonOAuth2Provider;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.registration.ClientRegistration;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.registration.ClientRegistrationRepository;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.registration.InMemoryClientRegistrationRepository;

@Configuration
class GoogleRegistration {
  @Bean
  ClientRegistrationRepository registrations(
      @Value("${GOOGLE_CLIENT_ID}") String id,
      @Value("${GOOGLE_CLIENT_SECRET}") String secret) {
    ClientRegistration google = CommonOAuth2Provider.GOOGLE
        .getBuilder("google").clientId(id).clientSecret(secret).build();
    return new InMemoryClientRegistrationRepository(google);
  }
}

Use this bean instead of the automatic Google registration properties, not next to them in the same learning project. This in-memory example loads environment variables when the app starts; it does not demonstrate live credential rotation. A dynamic repository needs careful caching, atomic updates, and an auditable secret source. The browser callback still needs to be registered at Google.

04

The signed-in user reaches the security context

After the provider redirects back and Spring Security completes authentication, the app has a local Authentication. You can inject it into a controller or use authorization rules just as with other login methods. A provider identity is not automatically an account in your own domain: decide how users are provisioned, linked, and assigned application permissions.

ProfileController.java · use a safe subset of the principal
import java.util.Map;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;

@RestController
class ProfileController {
  @GetMapping("/me")
  Map<String, String> me(Authentication authentication) {
    return Map.of("providerSubject", authentication.getName());
  }
}

Combine this controller with one of the login chains above. /me is protected by anyRequest().authenticated(). For more provider-specific fields, an OAuth2AuthenticationToken or OIDC principal can expose them after login; never serialize the entire principal, authorized client, session, or raw token as an API response.

05

A service can request its own token

For service-to-service calls, register a confidential client with the issuer for client_credentials and a narrow API scope. No browser, authorization redirect, or human login is involved. In chapter 14 the service-client registration has invoices.read; in chapter 15 the /invoices API requires SCOPE_invoices.read.

Use the OAuth 2 client starter along with web/security if this app also serves HTTP requests. The following properties are a separate service-client app, not the web-login app’s registration. The token endpoint and client credentials must match the issuer; never set openid as the service’s API permission. Secrets should come from the deployment environment.

application.properties · service client, separate app
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.invoice-service.provider=local-issuer
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.invoice-service.client-id=service-client
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.invoice-service.client-secret=${DEMO_SERVICE_CLIENT_SECRET}
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.invoice-service.client-authentication-method=client_secret_basic
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.invoice-service.authorization-grant-type=client_credentials
spring.security.oauth2.client.registration.invoice-service.scope=invoices.read
spring.security.oauth2.client.provider.local-issuer.token-uri=http://localhost:8080/oauth2/token
# For production: use the issuer's HTTPS token endpoint and a secret manager.

For a background job or service layer, use AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager instead of a request-scoped manager tied to a servlet request. A stable application principal lets the manager reuse an unexpired authorized client; an in-memory authorized-client service loses that cache on restart. Match caching, storage, rotation, and timeouts to your deployment.

ServiceClientConfiguration.java · manager for background calls
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.InMemoryOAuth2AuthorizedClientService;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.OAuth2AuthorizedClientProviderBuilder;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.registration.ClientRegistrationRepository;

@Configuration
class ServiceClientConfiguration {
  @Bean
  OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager clientManager(
      ClientRegistrationRepository registrations) {
    var service = new InMemoryOAuth2AuthorizedClientService(
        registrations);
    var manager = new AuthorizedClientServiceOAuth2AuthorizedClientManager(
        registrations, service);
    manager.setAuthorizedClientProvider(
        OAuth2AuthorizedClientProviderBuilder.builder()
            .clientCredentials().build());
    return manager;
  }
}
Inbound traffic is separateConfiguring an OAuth 2 client only handles outgoing token acquisition. If this service also exposes HTTP endpoints, configure and test its own inbound SecurityFilterChain; never turn an unauthenticated /token endpoint into a credential vending machine.
06

Send the token to the intended API

A useful client does not return the bearer token to a browser. A service or proxy obtains the authorized client, sends the token only to the intended resource server in an Authorization header, and returns business data. The API still verifies issuer, audience, expiry, and scope independently.

This Spring Framework 6.1+ RestClient example belongs in the same app as ServiceClientConfiguration and its properties, not the login app. For a local exercise the chapter 15 API listens on port 9090 and the issuer on 8080. It is an internal service method, deliberately not a public /token controller.

InvoiceProxy.java · call the protected API
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.OAuth2AuthorizeRequest;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.OAuth2AuthorizedClient;
import org.springframework.security.oauth2.client.OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.client.RestClient;

@Service
class InvoiceProxy {
  private final OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager;
  private final RestClient invoices = RestClient.builder()
      .baseUrl("http://localhost:9090").build();

  InvoiceProxy(OAuth2AuthorizedClientManager manager) {
    this.manager = manager;
  }

  String fetchInvoices() {
    var request = OAuth2AuthorizeRequest
        .withClientRegistrationId("invoice-service")
        .principal("invoice-service").build();
    OAuth2AuthorizedClient client = manager.authorize(request);
    if (client == null) {
      throw new IllegalStateException("Token acquisition failed");
    }
    return invoices.get().uri("/invoices")
        .headers(h -> h.setBearerAuth(
            client.getAccessToken().getTokenValue()))
        .retrieve().body(String.class);
  }
}
Keep the grant’s meaning. This token represents the service-client, not the HTTP caller; do not use it to make a request appear to come from a particular user. In production, use an HTTPS API address, explicit timeouts, safe error handling, scoped credentials, and audience checks on the resource server. Never log bearer strings or send one to a caller-selected URL.
✓

Keep these ideas

01oauth2Login() signs a person into a web app through a registered provider and a precise callback.
02Custom OIDC issuers can expose discovery metadata; client registration, PKCE, session cookies, and redirect URIs must still agree.
03A client-credentials token belongs to the service, not a user. An authorized-client manager acquires and reuses it.
04Keep tokens inside a trusted proxy and send them only to the intended API; never return them from a public demo endpoint.

Check your understanding

Does an OAuth 2 login make a browser session an API access token?

No. The app establishes a local authenticated session. Any access token has its own issuer, audience, scope, and intended resource; a browser session cookie is not a substitute.

Why does the custom issuer need a matching callback and PKCE?

The issuer only redirects to an exact registered callback, and chapter 14’s example requires a valid PKCE challenge and verifier for its authorization-code client. Both sides must agree or login fails.

Whose identity is represented by a client-credentials token?

The confidential client application’s. It does not prove a human signed in or permit a service to impersonate a caller.

Chapter 17 · Security for reactive applications

Secure the
whole stream.

Reactive code can resume on another thread. Its identity must follow the request through the publisher, not live in a thread-local variable. Spring Security supplies a WebFlux filter chain, reactive user services, method checks, and JWT resource-server support.

Reactor contextWebFlux rules9 book figures
Identity follows the work
Request + authenticationSTART
Reactor contextCARRY
Authorization + responseDECIDE

Never assume one request owns one thread.

Chapter seventeen

The big picture01 / Reactive model02 / Context, not threads03 / Users + Basic04 / Exchange rules05 / Method security06 / Reactive JWT APIQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 17, “Implementing security in reactive applications” (book pp. 347–369). All nine numbered figures are embedded. Examples replace the book’s plaintext passwords, broad permit-all rule, and obsolete resource-server grant.
The 60-second takeaway

Same decisions; a different execution model.

A WebFlux endpoint returns a publisher such as Mono or Flux. Spring Security authenticates and authorizes its HTTP exchange using SecurityWebFilterChain. When work moves between threads, the authentication lives in the reactive context; use ReactiveSecurityContextHolder, not servlet SecurityContextHolder or a hand-rolled ThreadLocal.

01

Publishers are the unit of work

The book contrasts a batch of milk bottled all at once with small batches delivered as they finish. Reactor’s Mono<T> emits zero or one value; Flux<T> emits zero or more. A subscriber triggers the pipeline. This model supports non-blocking composition but does not magically make CPU work faster or make a blocking database client non-blocking.

Mono

At most one result

Appropriate for a single user lookup, an authorization decision, or a one-value HTTP response.

Flux

A sequence of results

Useful for multiple values, provided upstream and downstream actually support streaming and backpressure.

For a dedicated reactive server use spring-boot-starter-webflux and spring-boot-starter-security. Avoid adding the servlet web starter to this learning project: if both MVC and WebFlux starters are present, Spring Boot normally chooses MVC. Do not call block() or subscribe() inside a WebFlux request handler to glue security to asynchronous work; compose publishers with map/flatMap instead.

02

Authentication travels with the reactive context

Servlet examples can rely on a security context associated with the processing thread. In a reactive pipeline different parts of one request may execute on different threads, while the same thread may handle different requests. A thread-local lookup can therefore select the wrong principal or none at all. Spring Security associates the context with the subscriber’s Reactor context.

When the security filters authenticate a request, ReactiveSecurityContextHolder.getContext() returns a Mono<SecurityContext>. Read it inside the returned publisher. The example below is the controller used with the Basic-auth configuration in section 03; the same principal lookup works with the JWT configuration in section 06.

ReactiveHelloController.java · read auth in the pipeline
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContext;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.ReactiveSecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

@RestController
class ReactiveHelloController {
  @GetMapping("/hello")
  Mono<String> hello() {
    return ReactiveSecurityContextHolder.getContext()
        .map(SecurityContext::getAuthentication)
        .map(auth -> "Hello " + auth.getName());
  }

  @GetMapping("/ciao")
  Mono<String> ciao() {
    return Mono.just("Ciao!");
  }
}

The protected /hello handler only runs after authentication under the matching security chain. If you later allow anonymous access, explicitly handle an empty context instead of treating an empty publisher as successful authorization. Prefer framework-managed context propagation; a detached subscription or manually spawned work may not preserve it.

03

Reactive user lookup, real password hashing

For HTTP Basic in WebFlux, AuthenticationWebFilter delegates to a ReactiveAuthenticationManager. A ReactiveUserDetailsService returns a Mono<UserDetails> for lookup. The book stores a literal 12345 password with NoOpPasswordEncoder; our learning variant hashes a password supplied by the environment before creating an in-memory user.

Use ReactiveHelloController from section 02 together with this single security class. Set DEMO_REACTIVE_PASSWORD before starting the app. The password is encoded once during configuration; a real user store should keep durable hashes and provide genuinely non-blocking retrieval, not just wrap a blocking JDBC call in Mono.just(...).

ReactiveBasicSecurity.java · WebFlux user and chain
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Value;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.web.server.ServerHttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.ReactiveUserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.MapReactiveUserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.web.server.SecurityWebFilterChain;

@Configuration
class ReactiveBasicSecurity {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder passwordEncoder() {
    return new BCryptPasswordEncoder();
  }

  @Bean
  ReactiveUserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder,
      @Value("${DEMO_REACTIVE_PASSWORD}") String password) {
    if (password.isBlank()) throw new IllegalArgumentException(
        "Set DEMO_REACTIVE_PASSWORD");
    return new MapReactiveUserDetailsService(User.withUsername("reader")
        .password(encoder.encode(password)).roles("READER").build());
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityWebFilterChain api(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    return http.authorizeExchange(ex -> ex
        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/ciao").permitAll()
        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/hello").hasRole("READER")
        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/report").authenticated()
        .anyExchange().denyAll())
      .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
      .build();
  }
}
Terminal · try the WebFlux rules locally
# Set a long random DEMO_REACTIVE_PASSWORD in the app's environment.
curl -i http://localhost:8080/ciao
curl -i http://localhost:8080/hello              # 401 without credentials
curl -i -u "reader:$DEMO_REACTIVE_PASSWORD" http://localhost:8080/hello
# Expect Ciao! for /ciao and Hello reader for authenticated /hello.
Local exercise onlyHTTP Basic sends reusable credentials on every request; use TLS in any shared environment. The hashed in-memory password and environment variable are for an isolated demo, not a substitute for a managed credential store, rate limiting, or lifecycle controls.
04

Authorize exchanges, not servlet requests

The reactive type is SecurityWebFilterChain, built with ServerHttpSecurity. Use authorizeExchange, pathMatchers, and anyExchange where the servlet stack would use authorizeHttpRequests, requestMatchers, and anyRequest. The Basic chain above allows a public /ciao, requires a role for /hello, and denies unlisted exchanges by default.

Authentication

Who is calling?

The filter verifies a password or bearer token and places an Authentication in reactive context. Missing or invalid credentials normally produce 401.

Authorization

May they do this?

The matching exchange or method policy checks roles, scopes and resource rules; valid credentials with insufficient rights normally produce 403.

When basic matchers are insufficient, access(...) can receive a Mono<Authentication> and an AuthorizationContext, returning a publisher of authorization decisions. Explicitly deny an empty authentication (for example with defaultIfEmpty) and inspect trusted request data only. The book’s time-of-day example illustrates the hook; a production rule must define time zone, clock source and failure behavior. Never use permitAll() as a blanket fallback for an API.

05

Guard methods in the reactive pipeline

Enable reactive method security and annotate a method returning Mono or Flux with @PreAuthorize. The check can protect a service even if it is called from more than one controller. The secure method must be invoked through Spring’s proxy: a call from another method on the same instance can bypass the interception.

The following additions work with the Basic security chain from section 03: it allows authenticated GET /report, while method security requires ROLE_READER before the service returns data. These are separate classes in the same app, not another SecurityWebFilterChain.

ReactiveReport.java · method-level role check
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreAuthorize;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.method.configuration.EnableReactiveMethodSecurity;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import reactor.core.publisher.Mono;

@Configuration
@EnableReactiveMethodSecurity
class ReactiveMethodSecurity { }

@Service
class ReportService {
  @PreAuthorize("hasRole('READER')")
  public Mono<String> report() {
    return Mono.just("Reader report");
  }
}

@RestController
class ReportController {
  private final ReportService reports;
  ReportController(ReportService reports) { this.reports = reports; }
  @GetMapping("/report")
  Mono<String> report() { return reports.report(); }
}

For more involved permissions, method expressions can inspect arguments or use an authorized service. Do not perform blocking lookups inside an expression on the event loop; use a reactive authorization strategy that preserves context and completes the decision before emitting sensitive data.

06

A reactive resource server still validates tokens

WebFlux can be an OAuth 2 resource server just like the chapter 15 MVC API. Add spring-boot-starter-oauth2-resource-server to the reactive web/security starters. The same core requirements apply: validate signature, issuer, expiry, audience, and scope. Only the filter-chain type and authentication flow are reactive.

This is a separate app configuration: replace ReactiveBasicSecurity and its in-memory user with the class and properties below; keep ReactiveHelloController but do not add ReactiveReport unless you adapt its role rules to JWT authorities. A sample chapter 14 service token carrying invoices.read can call /hello after the resource server validates it. The issuer runs on 8080 and this API on 9090.

ReactiveJwtSecurity.java · separate JWT API configuration
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.web.server.ServerHttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.web.server.SecurityWebFilterChain;

@Configuration
class ReactiveJwtSecurity {
  @Bean
  SecurityWebFilterChain api(ServerHttpSecurity http) {
    return http.authorizeExchange(ex -> ex
        .pathMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/hello")
            .hasAuthority("SCOPE_invoices.read")
        .anyExchange().denyAll())
      .oauth2ResourceServer(oauth -> oauth.jwt(Customizer.withDefaults()))
      .build();
  }
}
application.properties · local reactive resource server
server.port=9090
spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.issuer-uri=http://localhost:8080
# Once the issuer puts invoices-api in access-token aud, require it here:
# spring.security.oauth2.resourceserver.jwt.audiences=invoices-api
# Production: exact HTTPS issuer, appropriate audience, and narrow scopes.

Configure audience issuance at the issuer and enable the commented audience check before a real deployment; the chapter 14 study issuer does not necessarily set one for this API by default. An issuer-uri validates the expected issuer as well as discovering signing keys; a bare jwk-set-uri is not equivalent without an additional issuer validator. A parsed JWT is not a verified JWT.

Outdated book exerciseThe printed example adds spring-cloud-starter-oauth2, uses a Keycloak-era /auth/realms/.../certs URL, and requests a token with the password grant. Do not copy those steps into a new Spring Security resource server. The Boot resource-server starter plus trusted issuer metadata is sufficient for this JWT example; obtain tokens via a currently supported grant and verify issuer, audience and scope.
✓

Keep these ideas

01Mono and Flux model asynchronous work; blocking operations still need explicit treatment.
02Reactive authentication travels via Reactor context, not a servlet-style thread-local.
03SecurityWebFilterChain controls exchanges; reactive method security protects publisher-returning methods.
04Reactive JWT APIs must still check trusted issuer, audience, lifetime and actual permissions.

Check your understanding

Why not read servlet SecurityContextHolder from a WebFlux thread?

Reactive work can move threads and a worker can process multiple requests. Authentication is propagated through Reactor context; use ReactiveSecurityContextHolder inside the publisher chain.

Does returning Mono.just(blockingDatabaseCall()) make the database call non-blocking?

No. The blocking call runs immediately before the publisher is made and can stall an event loop. Use a truly non-blocking driver or isolate blocking work on an appropriate scheduler.

Is JWKS signature verification enough for the reactive JWT API?

No. Require the trusted issuer, valid time bounds, the intended API audience, and the scope or authority required for the operation.

Chapter 18 · Testing security configurations

Prove the
boundary.

A rule that looks secure is not enough. Exercise the anonymous, permitted, and forbidden paths; test authentication separately; then check CSRF, CORS, bearer-token behavior, and reactive endpoints before changes reach production.

MockMvc + WebTestClientAuth vs authorization10 book figures
A useful security regression test
No identity401
Wrong permission403
Correct permission200

Cover denied cases, not just the happy path.

Chapter eighteen

The big picture01 / Testable boundary02 / Mock identities03 / Stored + custom users04 / Method rules05 / Real authentication06 / Token tests07 / CSRF + CORS08 / WebTestClientQuick recap
Reading noteBased on chapter 18, “Testing security configurations” (book pp. 373–398). All ten numbered figures are embedded. Mock principals and bearer tokens bypass authentication; real credential and token-verification tests must be separate.
The 60-second takeaway

Test exactly the layer you mean to test.

@WithMockUser, user(), jwt(), and opaqueToken() prepare a test security context so you can focus on authorization; they do not prove passwords, signatures, issuer checks, or introspection. For authentication, send actual credentials through the filters. Use MockMvc for servlet apps and WebTestClient for WebFlux; include negative tests and run them in CI.

01

Give the examples a testable boundary

A regression suite helps catch a policy broken by a code or dependency change. The following small MVC fixture defines a protected GET, a CSRF-protected POST, a Basic user store, and an explicitly allowed browser origin. All servlet examples through section 07 assume this fixture unless a note says they belong to the separate JWT or opaque-token app.

pom.xml · test-scoped dependencies
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.boot</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-boot-starter-test</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>
<dependency>
  <groupId>org.springframework.security</groupId>
  <artifactId>spring-security-test</artifactId>
  <scope>test</scope>
</dependency>

Put this fixture in a small Spring Boot servlet app with spring-boot-starter-web and spring-boot-starter-security. It is an isolated testing example, not a new filter chain to add to the earlier chapter 15 or 17 applications. The fixed password is test-only and encoded; never ship this demo account or its credentials to production.

SecurityTestFixture.java · MVC endpoints and policy
import java.util.List;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;
import org.springframework.http.HttpMethod;
import org.springframework.security.config.Customizer;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.web.builders.HttpSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.config.annotation.method.configuration.EnableMethodSecurity;
import org.springframework.security.core.Authentication;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.User;
import org.springframework.security.core.userdetails.UserDetailsService;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.bcrypt.BCryptPasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.crypto.password.PasswordEncoder;
import org.springframework.security.provisioning.InMemoryUserDetailsManager;
import org.springframework.security.web.SecurityFilterChain;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.GetMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.PostMapping;
import org.springframework.web.bind.annotation.RestController;
import org.springframework.web.cors.CorsConfiguration;
import org.springframework.web.cors.CorsConfigurationSource;
import org.springframework.web.cors.UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource;

@Configuration
@EnableMethodSecurity
class SecurityTestFixture {
  @Bean
  PasswordEncoder encoder() { return new BCryptPasswordEncoder(); }

  @Bean
  UserDetailsService users(PasswordEncoder encoder) {
    return new InMemoryUserDetailsManager(User.withUsername("reader")
        .password(encoder.encode("local-test-password"))
        .authorities("read", "write").build());
  }

  @Bean
  SecurityFilterChain web(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http.cors(Customizer.withDefaults())
      .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
        .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.GET, "/hello").hasAuthority("read")
        .requestMatchers(HttpMethod.POST, "/hello").hasAuthority("write")
        .anyRequest().denyAll())
      .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults()).build();
  }

  @Bean
  CorsConfigurationSource corsSource() {
    var cors = new CorsConfiguration();
    cors.setAllowedOrigins(List.of("https://app.example.com"));
    cors.setAllowedMethods(List.of("GET", "POST"));
    cors.setAllowedHeaders(List.of("Content-Type", "X-CSRF-TOKEN"));
    cors.setAllowCredentials(true);
    var source = new UrlBasedCorsConfigurationSource();
    source.registerCorsConfiguration("/hello", cors);
    return source;
  }
}

@RestController
class GreetingController {
  @GetMapping("/hello")
  String hello(Authentication auth) { return "Hello " + auth.getName(); }
  @PostMapping("/hello")
  String save() { return "Saved"; }
}

The following JUnit 5 classes go under src/test/java in the same package as the Spring Boot application. In a real project, target your actual controller and configuration instead of shipping this fixture as application code. Protect credentials and filter test-only users out of deployed builds.

02

Mock identity to isolate authorization

A mock principal starts at the security context and skips password verification. Use @WithMockUser for a whole test method or user(...) as a per-request RequestPostProcessor. Both help prove whether a request is allowed given particular authorities; neither exercises your AuthenticationProvider.

This class targets SecurityTestFixture. It checks anonymous → 401, missing authority → 403, allowed authority → 200 and the exact body. read is an authority, not a role: roles="read" would create ROLE_read and test a different policy.

MockAuthorizationTests.java · anonymous, denied, allowed
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithMockUser;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;
import static org.springframework.security.test.web.servlet.request.SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.user;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.content;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class MockAuthorizationTests {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

  @Test
  void anonymousIsRejected() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/hello")).andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
  }

  @Test @WithMockUser(authorities = "other")
  void wrongAuthorityIsDenied() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/hello")).andExpect(status().isForbidden());
  }

  @Test @WithMockUser(username = "mary", authorities = "read")
  void readerIsAllowed() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/hello")).andExpect(status().isOk())
        .andExpect(content().string("Hello mary"));
  }

  @Test
  void perRequestUserWorksToo() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/hello").with(user("mary").authorities(
            () -> "read")))
        .andExpect(status().isOk());
  }
}
03

Stored users and custom test contexts

@WithUserDetails populates a test context by loading a user through a real UserDetailsService. This tests lookup integration and the authorization behavior of the retrieved user, but still bypasses password checking. When the application depends on a special Authentication shape, a WithSecurityContextFactory can construct one explicitly for a test.

StoredUserTests.java · lookup without password authentication
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithUserDetails;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.content;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class StoredUserTests {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;
  @Test @WithUserDetails("reader")
  void lookupAndAuthorize() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/hello")).andExpect(status().isOk())
        .andExpect(content().string("Hello reader"));
  }
}

This alternative test helper belongs under src/test/java, in the same package as the tests. It builds a TestingAuthenticationToken with the precise read authority needed by the fixture. It does not call the application’s real authentication manager. Keep authorization-sensitive principal claims under explicit test control.

WithTestReader.java · custom Authentication for a test
import java.lang.annotation.Retention;
import java.lang.annotation.RetentionPolicy;
import org.springframework.security.authentication.TestingAuthenticationToken;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContext;
import org.springframework.security.core.context.SecurityContextHolder;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithSecurityContext;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithSecurityContextFactory;

@Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME)
@WithSecurityContext(factory = TestReaderContextFactory.class)
@interface WithTestReader {
  String username() default "mary";
}

class TestReaderContextFactory
    implements WithSecurityContextFactory<WithTestReader> {
  @Override
  public SecurityContext createSecurityContext(WithTestReader annotation) {
    SecurityContext context = SecurityContextHolder.createEmptyContext();
    context.setAuthentication(new TestingAuthenticationToken(
        annotation.username(), null, "read"));
    return context;
  }
}

Apply @WithTestReader(username="mary") on a MockMvc test method to authorize GET /hello as Mary. If you need to test a particular custom principal type, create that type in your test fixture and place it in the factory’s Authentication; do not treat a synthetic principal as evidence that real login or token parsing works.

04

Test method security without HTTP

A service method protected with @PreAuthorize should be tested through the Spring-managed proxy. Inject the service bean rather than constructing it with new; mock identities are enough to test the rule. Distinguish anonymous, authenticated without permission, and authenticated with the exact required authority.

The fixture above already enables method security. Add this service to that small app, then place the JUnit class in its test sources. Tests run through the injected proxy; an internal self-call could bypass that proxy and deserves its own design review.

PublicationService.java · service-level rule
import org.springframework.security.access.prepost.PreAuthorize;
import org.springframework.stereotype.Service;

@Service
class PublicationService {
  @PreAuthorize("hasAuthority('write')")
  public String publish() { return "Published"; }
}
MethodRuleTests.java · proxy and authority checks
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.security.access.AccessDeniedException;
import org.springframework.security.core.AuthenticationException;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithMockUser;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals;
import static org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertThrows;

@SpringBootTest
class MethodRuleTests {
  @Autowired PublicationService service;

  @Test
  void anonymousFails() {
    assertThrows(AuthenticationException.class, service::publish);
  }

  @Test @WithMockUser(authorities = "read")
  void wrongAuthorityFails() {
    assertThrows(AccessDeniedException.class, service::publish);
  }

  @Test @WithMockUser(authorities = "write")
  void writerSucceeds() {
    assertEquals("Published", service.publish());
  }
}
05

Send credentials to test authentication

If you want to test password verification, do not supply a pre-authenticated mock user. Submit HTTP Basic credentials to MockMvc and let the configured filter, authentication manager, user service, and password encoder run. Test a good password and an invalid password with the same username.

BasicAuthenticationTests.java · through the filters
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;
import static org.springframework.security.test.web.servlet.request.SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.httpBasic;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.content;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class BasicAuthenticationTests {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

  @Test
  void correctPasswordWorks() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/hello").with(httpBasic("reader", "local-test-password")))
        .andExpect(status().isOk())
        .andExpect(content().string("Hello reader"));
  }

  @Test
  void incorrectPasswordFails() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/hello").with(httpBasic("reader", "wrong")))
        .andExpect(status().isUnauthorized());
  }
}

httpBasic(...) here only adds the HTTP Basic header to the request; the app must still authenticate it. For form login in an alternative chain, use formLogin() and test success/failure with the actual configured login endpoint and CSRF behavior. Never assume a mock-user or mock-token test has exercised the real credentials path.

06

Mock bearer tokens test policies, not signatures

Spring Security Test offers jwt() and opaqueToken() request postprocessors. They create an authenticated test context with controllable claims and authorities, making scope rules easy to exercise. But they do not run the JWT decoder, issuer/audience validator, or introspection network request.

The code below targets the chapter 15 JWT-mode /invoices resource server, not the Basic test fixture. Its controller receives a Jwt and requires SCOPE_invoices.read. The JWT postprocessor supplies this context directly: a deliberately wrong iss could still pass these authorization-only tests. Add separate tests using a real signed token and trusted test issuer to prove the validator rejects invalid issuer, signature, audience, expiry and algorithm.

JwtScopeTests.java · policy checks in the JWT-mode app
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.security.core.authority.SimpleGrantedAuthority;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;
import static org.springframework.security.test.web.servlet.request.SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.jwt;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.get;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class JwtScopeTests {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

  @Test
  void readScopeAllowsInvoices() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/invoices").with(jwt()
        .authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_invoices.read"))))
        .andExpect(status().isOk());
  }

  @Test
  void unrelatedScopeIsDenied() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(get("/invoices").with(jwt()
        .authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_other"))))
        .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
  }
}

For an opaque-token-mode endpoint that accepts an Authentication (not the JWT-specific @AuthenticationPrincipal Jwt controller above), use .with(opaqueToken().authorities(new SimpleGrantedAuthority("SCOPE_invoices.read"))) to check authorization. This skips the actual introspection response and revocation checks. Pair it with an issuer/introspection integration test or an explicit test double for those boundaries.

Do not mistake a mock for validationEven a token mock populated with an aud or iss claim does not prove those claims were checked. Tests for the decoder or introspector must drive the real authentication path and assert rejection of bad signatures, unexpected issuers/audiences, inactive tokens and insufficient scopes.
07

Check CSRF and CORS as browser boundaries

The fixture’s POST requires both the write authority and a CSRF token. Test the missing-token denial first, then add .with(csrf()) and verify the operation succeeds. A CORS preflight is an OPTIONS request with Origin and Access-Control-Request-Method; assert a specific trusted origin is reflected and an untrusted origin is refused.

BrowserBoundaryTests.java · CSRF and CORS outcomes
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.servlet.AutoConfigureMockMvc;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.http.HttpHeaders;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithMockUser;
import org.springframework.test.web.servlet.MockMvc;
import static org.springframework.security.test.web.servlet.request.SecurityMockMvcRequestPostProcessors.csrf;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.options;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.request.MockMvcRequestBuilders.post;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.content;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.header;
import static org.springframework.test.web.servlet.result.MockMvcResultMatchers.status;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureMockMvc
class BrowserBoundaryTests {
  @Autowired MockMvc mvc;

  @Test @WithMockUser(authorities = "write")
  void postWithoutCsrfIsDenied() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/hello")).andExpect(status().isForbidden());
  }

  @Test @WithMockUser(authorities = "write")
  void postWithCsrfSucceeds() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(post("/hello").with(csrf()))
        .andExpect(status().isOk()).andExpect(content().string("Saved"));
  }

  @Test
  void trustedOriginMayPreflightPost() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(options("/hello")
        .header(HttpHeaders.ORIGIN, "https://app.example.com")
        .header(HttpHeaders.ACCESS_CONTROL_REQUEST_METHOD, "POST"))
        .andExpect(status().isOk())
        .andExpect(header().string("Access-Control-Allow-Origin",
            "https://app.example.com"));
  }

  @Test
  void untrustedOriginCannotPreflight() throws Exception {
    mvc.perform(options("/hello")
        .header(HttpHeaders.ORIGIN, "https://evil.example")
        .header(HttpHeaders.ACCESS_CONTROL_REQUEST_METHOD, "POST"))
        .andExpect(status().isForbidden());
  }
}
Keep the threat model distinct. CSRF protection matters for browser sessions or other ambient credentials. A genuinely stateless API that accepts only explicit bearer tokens may use a different CSRF policy, but do not disable protection just to make a test pass. CORS limits what browsers expose to scripts; it is not server-side authentication, and credentialed responses must not use a wildcard allow-origin.
08

Use WebTestClient for reactive security

A chapter 17 WebFlux app uses SecurityWebFilterChain, so test its HTTP exchanges with WebTestClient. @WithMockUser and mockUser() still create a test identity; specify the role that the reactive chain actually requires. The example below assumes the chapter 17 ReactiveBasicSecurity and controller, where /hello needs ROLE_READER.

ReactiveRuleTests.java · WebFlux authorization
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test;
import org.springframework.beans.factory.annotation.Autowired;
import org.springframework.boot.test.autoconfigure.web.reactive.AutoConfigureWebTestClient;
import org.springframework.boot.test.context.SpringBootTest;
import org.springframework.security.test.context.support.WithMockUser;
import org.springframework.test.web.reactive.server.WebTestClient;
import static org.springframework.security.test.web.reactive.server.SecurityMockServerConfigurers.mockUser;

@SpringBootTest
@AutoConfigureWebTestClient
class ReactiveRuleTests {
  @Autowired WebTestClient client;

  @Test
  void anonymousCannotReadHello() {
    client.get().uri("/hello").exchange().expectStatus().isUnauthorized();
  }

  @Test @WithMockUser(roles = "READER")
  void annotatedReaderMayReadHello() {
    client.get().uri("/hello").exchange()
        .expectStatus().isOk().expectBody(String.class).isEqualTo("Hello user");
  }

  @Test
  void perRequestReaderMayReadHello() {
    client.mutateWith(mockUser("reader").roles("READER"))
        .get().uri("/hello").exchange()
        .expectStatus().isOk().expectBody(String.class).isEqualTo("Hello reader");
  }
}

The annotation and test configurer bypass the actual Basic-password check; add a separate WebTestClient request with real Basic credentials if you want to verify it. For a mutating WebFlux endpoint with CSRF protection, mutateWith(csrf()) is the analogous test helper. The chapter 17 example only exposes GET handlers, so do not paste a POST test into it without defining a POST route and policy first.

✓

Keep these ideas

01Mock users and tokens isolate authorization; tests with real credentials exercise authentication.
02Check anonymous, wrong permission and allowed paths for both web endpoints and proxied methods.
03Test CSRF denial and CORS exact-origin behavior; never substitute a browser policy for API authentication.
04Use MockMvc for MVC and WebTestClient for WebFlux; run tests after security or dependency changes.

Check your understanding

Can a passing jwt() mock test prove the API rejected an invalid signature?

No. The mock postprocessor supplies authentication without invoking the decoder. Exercise real token validation separately with signed test tokens and a trusted issuer or decoder setup.

What does @WithUserDetails cover that @WithMockUser does not?

It loads the principal from the configured UserDetailsService before the test. It still does not submit a password through the real authentication filter.

Why test a denied POST and a denied origin?

A happy-path assertion cannot prove the CSRF filter rejects missing tokens or CORS refuses an unapproved browser origin. Negative assertions check those boundaries directly.

A short companion to all 18 chapters

Start with the right version.

Spring’s current online reference may describe a newer release than the one in the 2024 book or in your application. Match the documentation to your Spring Boot, Spring Security, and Java versions; use API pages for exact signatures and reference guides for supported configuration patterns. The links below are external official sites, not content embedded in this offline guide.

A.1

Spring ecosystem references

The book points to the framework, security, and authorization-server documentation. Use each for a different question rather than assuming one guide covers every layer.

01

Spring Framework reference ↗

Web MVC and WebFlux, dependency injection, HTTP integration, and the foundational application model.

02

Spring Security reference ↗

Filter chains, authentication, authorization, OAuth 2 clients and resource servers, reactive security, and testing.

03

Spring Authorization Server API ↗

Class and method contracts for the authorization-server APIs used around chapter 14.

Reference versus API. The authorization-server link in the book is an API documentation destination, not a step-by-step installation guide. Consult the matching release’s reference material as well when setting up clients, keys, token policies, or OIDC endpoints. An API name alone does not define a secure deployment.
A.2

Java and testing references

Appendix A also supplies Java API and JUnit 5 documentation. Choose the Java API for the runtime or source level you target, not automatically the latest available release.

Java SE 17 API ↗The specific Java 17 API index cited by the book; useful for library contracts when using Java 17.
Java release documentation index ↗Pick the matching release if your project uses another Java version.
JUnit 5 user guide ↗Test lifecycle, assertions, extensions, and configuration behind the chapter 18 examples.

Appendix B

Source noteAppendix B, “Further reading,” printed pp. 400–402 (PDF pp. 425–427). Titles, authors, and publishers reflect the editions recommended in the book, not a claim about today’s newest edition.
Six recommendations · three paths

Read for the gap in your own work.

Need a stronger mental model for Spring? Start with framework and Boot. Tuning a data-heavy application? Choose a persistence book. Building a trustworthy regression suite after chapter 18? Turn to JUnit. The notes below summarize why each book is on the original list; they are not substitutes for the books themselves.

B.1

Spring foundations and Boot

These three recommendations complement security configuration with the framework concepts and application lifecycle around it.

01

Spring in Action, Sixth Edition

Craig Walls · Manning · 2022. Broader Spring foundations: dependency injection, AOP, data access, and web application design.

02

Spring Boot: Up and Running

Mark Heckler · O’Reilly Media · 2022. Boot’s auto-configuration, application setup, deployment model, and practical service development.

03

Spring Start Here

Laurențiu Spilcă · Manning · 2021. A gentler entry to core Spring, MVC, persistence, and the concepts on which security examples rely.

Suggested order: choose Spring Start Here if the container and MVC are still new; choose Spring in Action for a wider framework treatment; choose Spring Boot: Up and Running if application configuration and delivery are the immediate challenge. These are the book’s recommendations, not a ranking of all available Spring books.

B.2

Data access and persistence

Security decisions often depend on data: users, roles, tenant boundaries, and resource ownership. These two recommendations focus on the persistence layer that supplies it.

Performance path

High-Performance Java Persistence

Vlad Mihalcea · self-published · 2019. Hibernate and JPA performance, query and transaction behavior, batching, and database access patterns.

Spring Data path

Java Persistence with Spring Data and Hibernate, Third Edition

Cătălin Tudose · Manning · 2023. JPA mapping, repositories, querying, and Spring Data integration with Hibernate.

Bring security along. A faster query is not necessarily a safe query. Preserve authorization filters, tenant scoping, transaction boundaries, and least-privilege database access when improving persistence performance.
B.3

Testing as a discipline

Testing path

JUnit in Action, Third Edition

Cătălin Tudose · Manning · 2021 (as listed in appendix B). A deeper treatment of JUnit 5, assertions, test organization, mocking, integration tests, and testing Spring applications.

Use it alongside chapter 18 to expand beyond a few status assertions: design meaningful negative cases, make fixtures maintainable, and keep authentication tests distinct from mocked authorization tests. The book’s earlier chapter 18 introduction and this appendix print different publication years for this recommendation; the appendix lists 2021.

Edition noteThe publication years above are transcribed from appendix B. A title may have later editions or updated documentation; check the specific edition and supported framework versions before applying code unchanged.
